title: LLM-Assisted Empirical Software Engineering: Systematic Literature Review and Research Agenda
authors_or_org: Victoria Gomes et al.
summary: Systematic literature review of peer-reviewed papers (2020-2025) across 12 leading SE venues on how LLMs are used in empirical SE, yielding 50 primary studies. Maps tasks, lifecycle phases, workflow integration, benefits/limitations and reproducibility reporting.
key_claims: 69 LLM-assisted tasks identified, mainly in mining software repositories and controlled experiments, focused on classification, filtering and evaluation
LLM use is concentrated in data processing and analysis phases
Integration is largely automation-oriented, with limited decision-support use
Limitations reported include hallucinations, inconsistency, prompt sensitivity and reproducibility issues
Reporting practices are often incomplete

title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering: A Systematic Literature Review

authors_or_org: Sebastian Baltes et al.

key_claims: Eight guidelines: declare LLM usage and role; report model versions, configurations, customizations; document system and prompt design; report session traces (interaction logs and runtime traces); use suitable baselines, benchmarks, metrics; include an open LLM as a baseline; validate LLM outputs against human judgment; articulate limitations and mitigations
Seven study types; 22 contributing researchers
Seven study types: LLMs as annotators, as judges, for synthesis, as subjects, studying LLM usage in SE, LLMs for new SE tools, benchmarking LLMs for SE tasks.

Eight guidelines: (1) declare LLM usage and role; (2) report model versions, configurations, customizations; (3) document system and prompt design beyond the model; (4) report session traces (interaction logs and runtime traces); (5) suitable baselines, benchmarks, metrics; (6) include an open LLM as a baseline; (7) validate LLM outputs against human judgment; (8) articulate limitations and mitigations.
arXiv comment: 86 pages, accepted in Empirical Software Engineering.
relevance: The strongest existing reporting guidance in SE; it already goes beyond 'model + prompt' (session traces, human validation), which partly complicates the gap claim — but it does not require reporting delegated authority or human gates as process.

relevance: Closest SE tool to a 'human semantic gate' at question formulation (accept/edit/discard plus explicit Go/Pivot/Abort); whether those decisions are logged as provenance is not stated in what was read.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence for Software Engineering -- A Research Agenda
authors_or_org: Anh Nguyen-Duc, Beatriz Cabrero-Daniel, Adam Przybylek, Chetan Arora, Dron Khanna, Tomas Herda, Usman Rafiq, Jorge Melegati, Eduardo Guerra, Kai-Kristian Kemell, Mika Saari, Zheying Zhang, Huy Le, Tho Quan, Pekka Abrahamsson
summary: Literature review plus five months of focus groups producing a research agenda for GenAI in SE: 78 open research questions in 11 SE areas.
key_claims: 78 open research questions identified across 11 areas of software engineering
Common considerations include dependability and accuracy, data accessibility, transparency and sustainability
relevance: Agenda for GenAI as an object of SE research rather than as a participant in the research process; illustrates that the methodological use of AI by researchers was not yet on the agenda in 2023.

title: Can AI serve as a substitute for human subjects in software engineering research?
authors_or_org: Marco Aurélio Gerosa, Bianca Trinkenreich, Igor Steinmacher, Anita Sarma
summary: Vision paper on using LLM-generated synthetic data in SE study design (persona-based interviews, multi-persona focus groups, mega-persona surveys). Concludes AI can augment data gathering but cannot replace human subjects in some cases.
key_claims: Proposes persona-based prompting for interviews, multi-persona dialogue for focus groups and mega-persona responses for surveys
AI could augment aspects of data gathering but cannot replace the nuanced understanding of human subjects in some cases
Recommends integrating AI-generated and human-sourced data
Motivated by scale, labour intensity and participant-recruitment difficulty of traditional qualitative SE data collection
Proposes persona-based interviews, multi-persona focus groups and mega-persona survey responses
Expects an integrated approach where AI- and human-generated data coexist to be most effective.
relevance: Study-design stage in SE: choosing to substitute or augment participants with AI is a design decision whose rationale and configuration must be recorded; supports the thesis.

title: Get on the Train or be Left on the Station: Using LLMs for Software Engineering Research
authors_or_org: Bianca Trinkenreich, Fabio Calefato, Geir Kjetil Hanssen, Kelly Blincoe, Marcos Kalinowski, Mauro Pezzè, Paolo Tell, Margaret-Anne Storey
summary: Position paper from the 2nd Copenhagen Symposium on Human-Centered AI in SE using McLuhan's Tetrad to analyse how LLMs change SE research, including accelerated ideation and automated processes, and calling for frameworks and guidelines that keep human agency and oversight.
key_claims: Human oversight and interpretability are necessary for upholding scientific rigor
LLMs enhance research via accelerated ideation and automated processes but risk reversal effects when taken to extremes
Calls on the SE community to develop frameworks and guidelines to mitigate risks
Human oversight and interpretability are necessary for upholding scientific rigor.
Calls for frameworks and guidelines to mitigate risks of LLM use in SE research.
Argues human oversight and interpretability are necessary for upholding scientific rigor in LLM-supported SE research.
relevance: Strong SE-community support for the chapter's premise (human agency, need for frameworks); it calls for frameworks without supplying the process-level mechanisms the chapter proposes.

title: Generative AI and Empirical Software Engineering: A Paradigm Shift
authors_or_org: Christoph Treude, Margaret-Anne Storey
summary: Vision paper on how LLMs and agents disrupt empirical SE: the phenomena studied, methods and theories, data, and threats to validity. Notes that reproducibility becomes contingent on model updates and prompt contexts.
key_claims: Reproducibility of findings becomes contingent on model updates and prompt contexts
AI challenges foundational constructs such as 'developer', 'artifact' and 'interaction'
Calls for the ESE community to adapt questions, instruments and validation standards
Reproducibility of findings becomes contingent on model updates and prompt contexts.
Foundational constructs such as 'developer', 'artifact', and 'interaction' are challenged.
relevance: Supports the thesis that study design and validity must be rethought, and names prompt/model dependence; mainly concerns AI as studied phenomenon rather than AI running the research process.

title: ChatGPT application in Systematic Literature Reviews in Software Engineering: an evaluation of its accuracy to support the selection activity
authors_or_org: Katia Romero Felizardo, Marcia Heloísa Tavares de Figueredo Lima, Anderson Deizepe, Tayana Uchôa Conte, Igor Steinmacher
summary: Replicates the first selection stage of two SE SLRs with ChatGPT-4.0 using title, abstract and keywords, comparing to the original human selection.
key_claims: Accuracy 75.3% on SLR1 (101 correct / 33 incorrect) and 86.1% on SLR2 (386 correct / 62 incorrect)
Not advisable to completely outsource selection to ChatGPT; useful as a support tool
relevance: Core SE evidence that screening must stay human-gated; supports the thesis.

title: Beyond Accuracy: LLM Variability in Evidence Screening for Software Engineering SLRs
authors_or_org: Gilberto Sussumu Hida, Danilo Monteiro Ribeiro, Erika Yahata
summary: Compares 12 LLMs from 4 providers and 4 classical classifiers on screening for 2 real SE SLRs (518 papers), studying run-to-run variability, input metadata, and gain over classical models.
key_claims: LLMs showed substantial heterogeneity and residual non-determinism even at temperature zero
Removing the abstract consistently degraded performance; adding title/keywords gave no robust gains
No consistent, generalizable LLM superiority over classical models
Best mean accuracy: gpt-4o 0.83±0.03 (SLR1), gpt-4.1 0.84±0.05 (SLR2)
relevance: Strong support: non-determinism at temperature zero means model+prompt disclosure cannot reproduce screening decisions; the authors call for explicit reporting of variability and input configuration and justify adoption by governance constraints.

title: Class Imbalance and Batch Effects in LLM-Based Screening for Systematic Reviews
authors_or_org: Gilberto Sussumu Hida, Danilo Monteiro Ribeiro, Clayton Suguio Hida
summary: Experiment over five reviews comparing individual vs batch LLM screening, with and without prevalence metadata.
key_claims: No evidence that prevalence metadata improves performance
Batch processing produced larger behavioural changes that varied with class prevalence
Aggregate and item-level analyses did not always coincide
relevance: Shows that an operational choice (batching) silently changes decisions; such pipeline parameters are part of the process that must be recorded, supporting the thesis.

title: Observing the Conduct of Systematic Reviews with Generative AI Support: An Experience Report from a Graduate Software Engineering Course
authors_or_org: Danilo Monteiro Ribeiro, Gilberto Sussumu Hida
summary: Observational experience report: ten SE doctoral students in three groups piloted secondary studies with and without ChatGPT assistants; observations, artifacts and interaction threads were analysed.
key_claims: LLMs reduced initial barriers and made methodological problems more explicit
LLMs also favoured excessive delegation, superficial validation and a shift of focus from the SLR to the tool
Use should be accompanied by human supervision, decision records and critical reflection
relevance: Very close to the chapter's gap: explicitly names 'decision records' and 'excessive delegation'. Supports the thesis; small, educational sample.

title: SESR-Eval: Dataset for Evaluating LLMs in the Title-Abstract Screening of Systematic Reviews
authors_or_org: Aleksi Huotala, Miikka Kuutila, Mika Mäntylä
summary: Benchmark of 34,528 labelled primary studies from 24 SE secondary studies, used to evaluate 9 LLMs on title-abstract screening.
key_claims: 34,528 labelled primary studies from 24 SE secondary studies (from 169 candidate SR artifacts)
Differences between secondary studies exceed differences between LLMs
Cost under $40 per secondary study even for the most expensive model
LLMs not yet recommended for automating title-abstract screening; none achieved high recall with reasonable precision
relevance: Supports the thesis; also shows that SR replication packages are rarely reusable (24 of 169 suitable), relevant to executable reproducibility.

title: AISysRev -- LLM-based Tool for Title-abstract Screening
authors_or_org: Aleksi Huotala, Miikka Kuutila, Olli-Pekka Turtio, Simo Sipilä, Mika Mäntylä
summary: Containerized web tool for LLM title-abstract screening (multiple providers or local models, zero/few-shot), with manual screening interfaces that show LLM output as guidance; trialled on 137 papers.
key_claims: Screening speed typically 100–300 papers per minute
Papers fall into Easy Includes, Easy Excludes, Boundary Includes, Boundary Excludes
Boundary cases, where LLMs err, require human intervention
relevance: Concrete instance of a human gate on boundary cases; relevant as a design pattern, though logging/provenance of the human overrides is not described in what was read.

title: Understanding LLMs in Title-Abstract Screening: From Disagreements to Recommendations
authors_or_org: Mika Mäntylä, Patricia Matsubara, Katia Romero Felizardo, Miikka Kuutila, Marco Gerosa, Savio de Sousa Sampaio, Tayana Conte, Igor Steinmacher
summary: Analyses human–LLM disagreements in title-abstract screening across six SE reviews and over 1,000 papers.
key_claims: Disagreement has recurring identifiable causes: boundary ambiguity in key terms, keyword overemphasis, incorrect topic inference
Kappa between 0.52 and 0.77
Recommends semantic validation before deployment, multiple concurrent LLMs, and prioritized review of borderline decisions
relevance: Directly supports 'human semantic gates': recommends semantic validation and borderline review, i.e. a gate placed where meaning is ambiguous.

title: Towards LLM Accelerated Rapid Reviews for Software Tool Discovery -- Case for Log Anomaly Detection
authors_or_org: Jesse Nyyssölä, Hamza Bin Mazhar, Alexander Bakhtin, Matteo Esposito, Nana Reinikainen, Yuqing Wang, Ying Song, Davide Taibi, Mika Mäntylä
summary: Workflow combining LLM screening with coding agents to find and run software tools described in the literature on log anomaly detection.
key_claims: 3,233 Scopus papers screened by LLM to 569 candidates; 470 downloaded; 83 tools identified; 24 ran successfully
Roughly 4 hours of human effort and 12 hours of LLM computation
Future work: formalize the approach as reusable agent skills
relevance: Shows agentic SE literature work already running end-to-end with minimal human time; complicates the thesis on efficiency grounds and illustrates how much delegated work a short human-effort figure hides.

title: LLM4SCREENLIT: Recommendations on Assessing the Performance of Large Language Models for Screening Literature in Systematic Reviews
authors_or_org: Lech Madeyski, Barbara Kitchenham, Martin Shepperd
summary: Methodological paper arguing standard confusion-matrix metrics mislead under imbalanced, cost-asymmetric screening; proposes a Weighted Matthews Correlation Coefficient and audits 29 papers on three SE datasets.
key_claims: Only 10% of 29 papers reported MCC; 24% gave complete confusion matrices
None of five papers claiming workload savings quantified false-negative costs
Accuracy-optimized model lost 63.3% of relevant evidence vs 5.8% under WMCC
Recommends reporting 'Lost Evidence', full confusion matrices, and routing unclassifiable outputs to human review
relevance: Strong support: reporting of LLM-assisted screening in SE is incomplete and the metric choice itself is a governance decision; recommends human review for unclassifiable outputs.

title: Assessing the Ability of ChatGPT to Screen Articles for Systematic Reviews
authors_or_org: Eugene Syriani, István Dávid, Gauransh Kumar
venue: arXiv (published version: 'Screening articles for systematic reviews with ChatGPT', Journal of Computer Languages 80, 2024, DOI 10.1016/j.cola.2024.101287)
summary: Assesses consistency, classification performance and generalizability of ChatGPT screening on SE systematic-review datasets, compared with traditional SR-automation classifiers.
key_claims: ChatGPT is a viable option to automate SR screening but requires careful integration considerations
Journal version: up to 82% accuracy; best prompts specify exclusion criteria and avoid negative shots
relevance: Early SE evidence leaning toward automation; complicates the thesis somewhat, while its emphasis on consistency points to run-to-run variability as a recordable property.

title: On the road to interactive LLM-based systematic mapping studies
authors_or_org: Kai Petersen, Jan M. Gerken
summary: Solution proposal by the author of the SE mapping-study guidelines, outlining agent and prompting strategies for each step of an LLM-supported, interactive mapping study.
key_claims: Proposes strategies for each mapping-study step using agents and prompting
Calls for holistic solutions for LLM-supported mapping studies
relevance: Shows SE secondary-study methodologists moving toward agentic mapping studies; the proposal is about capability, so it leaves open how agent steps are recorded and reviewed.

title: Comparing LLMs and Proposing an ML-Based Approach for Search String Generation in Systematic Literature Reviews
authors_or_org: Diogo Adário Marassi, Juliana Alves Pereira, Katia Romero Felizardo
summary: Evaluates search strings generated by Llama-8B, Gemma-12B and Mistral-Nemo-12B against a published SLR and proposes a semi-automated ML pipeline plus a reproducible evaluation framework.
key_claims: LLM-generated search strings are inconsistent and sensitive to input conditions
Proposes a standardized reproducible evaluation framework for AI search-string generation
relevance: The search string is the reproducibility anchor of an SLR; its LLM generation is shown to be unstable, so the generation step itself needs recording.

title: Generative AI in Evidence-Based Software Engineering: A White Paper
authors_or_org: Matteo Esposito, Andrea Janes, Davide Taibi, Valentina Lenarduzzi
summary: Vision white paper on the role of generative AI in evidence-based SE, motivated by the growing cost of SLRs and mapping studies, announcing a suite of models to support EBSE researchers.
key_claims: Plans creation and empirical validation of a suite of models to support EBSE researchers
relevance: Agenda-level SE source pushing GenAI into EBSE; offers no governance or provenance model.

title: System for systematic literature review using multiple AI agents: Concept and an empirical evaluation
authors_or_org: Abdul Malik Sami, Zeeshan Rasheed, Kai-Kristian Kemell, Muhammad Waseem, Terhi Kilamo, Mika Saari, Anh Nguyen-Duc, Kari Systä, Pekka Abrahamsson
summary: Multi-agent LLM system intended to fully automate SLRs: search-string generation, title filtering, abstract summarization and analysis against predefined research questions. Code released.
key_claims: Aims to fully automate the SLR workflow from topic to analysis
Claims substantial time and effort reduction while maintaining comprehensiveness and precision
relevance: Example of the 'fully automated SLR' direction from SE researchers; claims are not accompanied by a decision-level audit trail, illustrating the gap.

title: Investigating the Use of LLMs for Evidence Briefings Generation in Software Engineering
authors_or_org: Mauro Marcelino, Marcos Alves, Bianca Trinkenreich, Bruno Cartaxo, Sérgio Soares, Simone D.J. Barbosa, Marcos Kalinowski
summary: Registered report with a controlled experimental protocol comparing RAG-generated evidence briefings with human-made ones on content fidelity, ease of understanding and usefulness.
key_claims: Protocol evaluates content fidelity, understandability and usefulness against human-made briefings
Results pending at submission
relevance: Synthesis/communication stage of secondary studies; uses a registered-report design, itself a governance mechanism (pre-commitment) relevant to the chapter.

title: SLRMentor: An LLM-Based Tool Supporting Learning of SLR in Software Engineering
authors_or_org: Rodolfo Gil-Pereira, Ronnie de Souza Santos, Cleyton Magalhães, Italo Santos
summary: Conversational assistant supporting SLR planning in SE (search strings, inclusion/exclusion criteria) with explanations grounded in established guidelines; piloted with graduate students.
key_claims: Helps clarify the SLR process and planning decisions and lowers barriers for novices
Still requires active methodological judgement
relevance: Relevant for the educator audience; planning decisions are AI-assisted, which raises the question of recording which criteria were AI-suggested.

title: Preliminary Guidelines for Using and Evaluating GenAI Tools to Support Systematic Literature Reviews
authors_or_org: Barbara Kitchenham, Sebastián Pizard, Lech Madeyski, Ronnie de Souza Santos, Martin Shepperd, David Budgen
summary: Guidelines from the originators of SE SLR methodology: reviews existing guidance and proposes GUEST (GenAI Use and Evaluation in SLR Tasks), process recommendations for planning, conducting and reporting GenAI-supported SLRs.
key_claims: Proposes the GUEST framework for planning, conducting and reporting
GenAI requires human oversight and is not currently capable of unsupervised systematic studies
relevance: The most important SE-specific comparator for the chapter: an existing process-level guideline for one stage (SLRs). The chapter must position against it (generalize across the lifecycle; provenance and bounded authority beyond reporting).

title: Large language models for conducting systematic reviews: on the rise, but not yet ready for use—a scoping review
authors_or_org: Judith-Lisa Lieberum, Markus Toews, Maria-Inti Metzendorf, Felix Heilmeyer, Waldemar Siemens, Christian Haverkamp, Daniel Böhringer, Joerg J Meerpohl, Angelika Eisele-Metzger
summary: Scoping review of LLM applications in systematic-review conduct in health research (37 LLM articles included).
key_claims: LLM approaches covered 10 of 13 defined SR steps, most often literature search (41%), study selection (38%) and data extraction (30%)
GPT used in 89% of studies; validation studies predominated (57%)
Authors rated LLM use promising in 54%, neutral 24%, non-promising 22%
relevance: Cross-disciplinary maturity baseline: experimental and not yet validated; supports the thesis.

title: Automation of Systematic Reviews with Large Language Models
authors_or_org: Christian Cao, Rohit Arora, Paul Cento, et al. (incl. Andrea C. Tricco, David Moher, Niklas Bobrovitz)
summary: Validation of otto-SR, an end-to-end LLM workflow for screening, extraction and risk-of-bias, benchmarked against graduate-level humans, then used to reproduce and update an issue of 12 Cochrane reviews.
key_claims: Screening: 96.7% sensitivity, 97.9% specificity (humans 81.7% / 98.1%)
Data extraction accuracy 93.1% vs human 79.7%
Reproduced and updated 12 Cochrane reviews (146,276 citations); a search snippet reports ~two days for ~12 work-years of work (NOT in the medRxiv abstract v1-v4; unverified)
Otto-SR-based meta-analyses yielded newly significant estimates in 2 reviews and negated significance in 1; all discrepancies underwent dual human review
relevance: The strongest complicating source: an agentic pipeline outperforms humans on several SR tasks. Yet its validation relied on dual human review of discrepancies, and changed conclusions show why the pipeline's decisions need provenance.

title: Position Statement on Artificial Intelligence (AI) Use in Evidence Synthesis Across Cochrane, the Campbell Collaboration, JBI, and the Collaboration for Environmental Evidence 2025
authors_or_org: Ella Flemyng, Anna Noel-Storr, Biljana Macura, Gerald Gartlehner, James Thomas, Joerg J Meerpohl, Zoe Jordan, Jan Minx, Angelika Eisele-Metzger, Candyce Hamel, Paweł Jemioło, Kylie Porritt, Matthew Grainger
venue: Campbell Systematic Reviews 21(4): e70074 (co-published in several journals)
summary: Joint position statement from four evidence-synthesis organisations endorsing RAISE: authors remain accountable, AI must be used with human oversight, and any AI use that makes or suggests judgements must be fully reported.
key_claims: 'An author is accountable for the content, methods, and findings of their evidence synthesis, including the decision to use AI'
'AI and automation in evidence synthesis should be used with human oversight'
'Any use of AI or automation that makes or suggests judgements should be fully and transparently reported'
Required disclosures: AI system names, versions and dates; purpose and stages affected; justification of methodological soundness; financial interests; limitations and biases
relevance: Mature, outside-SE precedent. Supports the thesis (oversight, accountability) but also partly complicates the gap claim: disclosure here already extends to judgement-making uses, stages affected and justification, not only model+prompt.

title: Responsible use of AI in evidence SynthEsis (RAISE): recommendations and guidance
authors_or_org: James Thomas, Ella Flemyng, Anna Noel-Storr, et al. (RAISE working group)
summary: Living guidance in three documents: RAISE 1 gives role-specific recommendations for eight roles in the evidence-synthesis ecosystem; RAISE 2 covers building and evaluating AI tools; RAISE 3 covers selecting and using AI tools, including ethical, legal and regulatory issues.
key_claims: RAISE 1 covers eight roles: evidence synthesists, methodologists, AI tool development teams, producing organisations, publishers, funders, users, trainers
RAISE 2: building, validating and evaluating AI evidence-synthesis tools and reporting evaluations
RAISE 3: assessing, selecting and using tools
Search results: most recent version 'RAISE 2026 1' updated 13 March 2026
relevance: Role-based responsibilities across an ecosystem are close in spirit to 'bounded authority'; the chapter should cite RAISE as the mature evidence-synthesis precedent and argue that SE lacks an equivalent spanning the whole empirical lifecycle.

title: Documenting artificial intelligence use in evidence synthesis is necessary, but not sufficient
authors_or_org: Kristen L. Scotti
summary: Commentary on a case study (Long et al.) that documented prompts and failure modes and published an SOP. Argues the real value lies in how cognitive labour was distributed: AI did bounded tasks while inclusion and extraction stayed human-led.
key_claims: AI tools were integrated only for bounded tasks; inclusion decisions and data extraction remained human-led
Cognitive offloading of decision-making to GenAI is difficult to do responsibly
The case study had no non-AI baseline; efficiency claims rest on team experience
relevance: Almost a direct statement of the chapter's thesis from outside SE (documentation is not enough; bounded tasks plus human-led decisions); good for the gap paragraph and for showing the idea is not idiosyncratic.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Automation in Evidence Synthesis: An Investigation of Methods Employed in Cochrane, Campbell Collaboration, and Environmental Evidence Reviews
authors_or_org: Kristen L. Scotti, Sarah M. Nielsen Young, Melanie A. Gainey, Haoyong Lan
summary: Audit of automation/ML use and reporting in 2,271 evidence syntheses (2017–2024) from Cochrane, Campbell and Environmental Evidence.
key_claims: Only ~5% explicitly reported using ML, mostly for screening
~12% used ML-enabled tools but ~90% of those did not clarify whether ML functionality was actually used
Living reviews showed higher ML integration (~15%)
relevance: Even in the best-governed review communities, reporting cannot tell whether the AI function was used; strong evidence for the reporting gap.

title: Reassessing Large Language Model Boolean Query Generation for Systematic Reviews
authors_or_org: Shuai Wang, Harrisen Scells, Bevan Koopman, Guido Zuccon
summary: Reproduces both the original ChatGPT Boolean-query study (Wang et al., SIGIR 2023) and a later reproducibility study (Staudinger et al.) whose findings diverged because it overlooked query validation, output formatting constraints and example selection.
key_claims: A prior reproducibility study diverged significantly from the original because it omitted validation of generated queries, output formatting constraints and selection of CoT examples
Query effectiveness varies significantly across models and prompt designs
Prompt design and model selection are key drivers
relevance: Direct evidence that disclosing the model and the prompt did not suffice to reproduce an LLM-assisted SR step; the unreported intermediate steps (validation, formatting, example choice) mattered. Strong support for the thesis.

title: Language agents achieve superhuman synthesis of scientific knowledge
authors_or_org: Michael Skarlinski, Sam Cox, Jon M. Laurent, James D. Braza, Michaela M. Hinks, Michael J. Hammerling, Manvitha Ponnapati, Samuel G. Rodriques, Andrew Dickson White
summary: PaperQA2, a literature agent, evaluated against subject-matter experts on retrieval, summarization and contradiction detection; introduces LitQA2.
key_claims: PaperQA2 matches or exceeds expert performance on three literature research tasks
Its cited summaries are more accurate than human-written Wikipedia articles
Identifies 2.34 ± 1.99 contradictions per paper in biology; 70% validated by experts
relevance: Complicates the thesis: claims superhuman literature synthesis. Still, validation was by human experts, and contradictions were only 70% valid, so human gates remain necessary.

title: Synthesizing scientific literature with retrieval-augmented language models
authors_or_org: Akari Asai, Jacqueline He, Rulin Shao, Weijia Shi, et al. (incl. Luke Zettlemoyer, Graham Neubig, Daniel S. Weld, Hannaneh Hajishirzi)
summary: OpenScholar, an open retrieval-augmented LM over 45 million open-access papers, evaluated on ScholarQABench (2,967 expert queries).
key_claims: GPT-4o hallucinates citations 78–90% of the time; OpenScholar reaches citation accuracy on par with human experts
OpenScholar-8B outperforms GPT-4o by 6.1% and PaperQA2 by 5.5% on correctness
Experts preferred OpenScholar responses over expert-written ones 51% (8B) and 70% (GPT-4o variant) of the time
relevance: Two-sided: supports the hallucination concern (78–90% citation hallucination for a general model) and complicates it (open, released artifacts reach expert parity). Open release of datastore and code is a reproducibility practice worth citing.

title: SciLitBench: Benchmark and Design Principles for LLM-Powered Systematic Literature Reviews
authors_or_org: Miguel Zabaleta, Baihan Lin
summary: Multi-stage benchmark covering title/abstract screening, full-text screening and schema-guided extraction (42,981 records, 1,012 full texts) evaluated on 22 open-weight LLMs.
key_claims: Explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria improve title/abstract screening F2 by 28.8%; researcher-authored rationales improve full-text screening by 15%
Extraction accuracy falls from 0.97 (publication year) to 0.37 Jaccard (computational approach)
Strongest models recover only 30% of annotated evaluation evidence and 25% of limitations
relevance: Shows extraction and synthesis are far less reliable than screening, so later SLR stages need stronger gates; human-authored rationales measurably help.

title: Completing A Systematic Review in Hours instead of Months with Interactive AI Agents
authors_or_org: Rui Qiu, Shijie Chen, Yu Su, Po-Yin Yen, Han-Wei Shen
summary: InsightAgent: human-centred multi-agent system for SRs with visualizations of the corpus and agent trajectories so users can monitor actions and give real-time feedback; user study with 9 medical professionals.
key_claims: Visualization and interaction improved SR quality by 27.2%, reaching 79.7% of human-written quality
User satisfaction improved by 34.4%
About 1.5 hours for a clinician to complete a review
relevance: Making agent trajectories visible to the human is a step toward inspectable process; the trajectories serve live monitoring, not archived provenance.

title: Breaking the Silence: the Threats of Using LLMs in Software Engineering
authors_or_org: June Sallou, Thomas Durieux, Annibale Panichella
summary: New-ideas paper opening discussion of threats to validity of LLM-based SE research: closed-source models, data leakage between training data and evaluation data, and reproducibility of LLM-based findings. Proposes guidelines for SE researchers and LM providers, illustrated with test-case generation.
key_claims: Names three threat families: closed-source models, training/evaluation data leakage, reproducibility.
Proposes guidelines for both SE researchers and LLM providers.
Identifies closed-source models, training-data leakage, and reproducibility of findings as key threats.
Proposes guidelines aimed at both SE researchers and LM providers.
relevance: Canonical statement of MSR/SE-specific LLM threats (leakage, non-determinism, closed models); supports the thesis but treats the LLM as an evaluated tool, not as a research participant whose decisions need recording.

title: Agentic Repository Mining: A Multi-Task Evaluation
authors_or_org: Johannes Härtel
summary: Compares LLM agents that explore repositories via bash commands against plain LLMs given pre-engineered context for MSR classification tasks (commits, reviews, code lines, repositories). Agents achieve competitive accuracy and are more robust to context size; manual diagnosis of disagreements reveals ambiguous specifications and ground-truth labels produced under limited context.
key_claims: Four tasks, eight approach configurations, 4943 classifications.
Agents achieve competitive accuracy despite retrieving their own context; main advantage is robustness (no context-window overflow).

Manual diagnosis of 100 disagreement cases reveals specification ambiguities and labels produced under limited context; accuracy against such ground truth may underestimate broader-context approaches.
relevance: Direct evidence that agents now perform MSR data curation autonomously, choosing what context to retrieve: exactly the delegated, unrecorded decisions the chapter targets. Also complicates 'human ground truth' as the validation anchor.

title: Leveraging GPT-like LLMs to Automate Issue Labeling
authors_or_org: Giuseppe Colavito, Filippo Lanubile, Nicole Novielli, Luigi Quaranta
summary: Investigates whether GPT-like decoder models can classify issue reports without the labeled data needed to fine-tune BERT-like models. Reports that GPT-like models can correctly classify issue reports in the absence of labeled training data.
key_claims: GPT-like models classify issue reports without labeled fine-tuning data (zero/few-shot).
A search snippet (attribution uncertain) reports zero-shot GPT-3.5 comparable to supervised models on a 400-issue dataset.
relevance: Representative of LLM labeling of MSR artifacts that silently replaces a human-labelled dataset; useful as an example of where the labeling decision is delegated.

title: Benchmarking large language models for automated labeling: The case of issue report classification
authors_or_org: Giuseppe Colavito, Filippo Lanubile, Nicole Novielli
summary: Journal benchmark of LLMs for automated labeling of GitHub issue reports: 22 generative decoder-only LLMs and 2 BERT-like encoder-only baselines evaluated on two GitHub-issue datasets for performance, response time, hardware requirements and response quality. Generative LLMs show zero-shot potential but vary across datasets and are resource-heavy; fine-tuned BERT-like models are more consistent.
key_claims: 22 generative decoder-only LLMs and 2 BERT-like encoder-only baselines evaluated on two GitHub-issue datasets.
Generative LLM performance varies significantly across datasets and requires substantial compute; BERT-like models are more consistent with lower resource needs.
relevance: Shows LLM-as-labeler is being benchmarked as a data-curation step in MSR; does not address provenance of the labeling process.

title: ChatGPT outperforms crowd workers for text-annotation tasks
authors_or_org: Fabrizio Gilardi, Meysam Alizadeh, Maël Kubli
summary: Compares zero-shot ChatGPT against MTurk crowd workers and trained annotators on 6,183 tweets and news articles for relevance, stance, topic and frame detection. ChatGPT is more accurate than crowd workers and more internally consistent than both crowd workers and trained annotators, at a fraction of the cost.
key_claims: n = 6,183 tweets and news articles, four samples.
Zero-shot ChatGPT accuracy exceeds crowd workers by about 25 percentage points on average.
ChatGPT intercoder agreement exceeds both crowd workers and trained annotators for all tasks.
Per-annotation cost under $0.003, about thirty times cheaper than MTurk.
relevance: COMPLICATES the thesis: strong evidence that LLM annotation can beat humans on cost and consistency; the chapter must argue that high agreement does not remove the need to record and gate the delegation. Cited by the anchor SLR.

title: Testing the Reliability of ChatGPT for Text Annotation and Classification: A Cautionary Remark
authors_or_org: Michael V. Reiss
summary: Tests the consistency of ChatGPT's zero-shot annotation under varying model parameters, prompt wordings and repeated identical inputs on a news/not-news website classification task. Finds consistency can fall below scientific reliability thresholds and advises against unsupervised use.
key_claims: Minor prompt-wording changes or repeating identical input can change outputs.
Consistency can fall short of scientific thresholds for reliability.
Pooling repeated outputs improves reliability; unsupervised application for annotation is not recommended.
relevance: Supports the thesis: non-determinism means the run configuration and repetitions are part of the evidence and must be recorded.

title: ChatGPT-4 Outperforms Experts and Crowd Workers in Annotating Political Twitter Messages with Zero-Shot Learning
authors_or_org: Petter Törnberg
summary: Compares ChatGPT-4 with expert classifiers and crowd workers on classifying the political affiliation of US politicians' tweets from the 2020 election against a ground truth. ChatGPT-4 achieves higher accuracy and reliability and equal or lower bias than the human annotators.
key_claims: ChatGPT-4 achieves higher accuracy, higher reliability, and equal or lower bias than expert and crowd human classifiers.
Correctly annotates messages requiring contextual reasoning and inference about author intent.
relevance: COMPLICATES the thesis from outside SE: claims LLMs exceed experts even on interpretive annotation, which the chapter must address rather than ignore.

title: The Alternative Annotator Test for LLM-as-a-Judge: How to Statistically Justify Replacing Human Annotators with LLMs
authors_or_org: Nitay Calderon, Roi Reichart, Rotem Dror
summary: Proposes the Alternative Annotator Test (alt-test), a statistical procedure using a modest human-annotated subset to justify replacing human annotators with an LLM, plus a measure for comparing LLM judges. Evaluated on ten datasets with six LLMs and four prompting techniques.
key_claims: Ten datasets (language and vision-language), six LLMs, four prompting techniques.
LLMs can sometimes replace humans; closed-source LLMs such as GPT-4o outperformed the open-source LLMs examined.
Prompting technique materially changes judge quality.
relevance: Provides a formal, recordable gate for the substitution decision; supports the thesis that delegation must be justified, and offers a concrete mechanism the chapter can cite as a validation pattern.

title: From brittle to robust: Improving LLM annotations for SE optimization
authors_or_org: Lohith Senthilkumar, Tim Menzies
summary: Proposes SynthCore, an ensemble of independent few-shot LLM labeling sessions, to label data for SE multi-objective optimization tasks where single-LLM labeling has blind spots. Tested on 49 tasks; optimizations found with LLM-only labels beat state-of-the-art alternatives.
key_claims: 49 SE multi-objective optimization tasks.
Optimizations were made using data labeled by LLMs without any human opinions.
Ensembles of separated few-shot sessions outperform Gaussian Process Models, Tree of Parzen Estimators and active learners.
relevance: COMPLICATES the thesis: demonstrates a fully human-free labeling pipeline in EMSE; supports it only in that robustness came from an explicit, recordable aggregation design.

title: Promises, Perils, and (Timely) Heuristics for Mining Coding Agent Activity
authors_or_org: Romain Robbes, Théo Matricon, Thomas Degueule, André Hora, Stefano Zacchiroli
summary: Documents promises, perils and heuristics gathered from studying coding-agent activity on GitHub, noting agents leave visible traces in repositories that MSR techniques can study.
key_claims: Coding agents saw very rapid adoption in 2025 and leave visible traces in software repositories.
relevance: Adjacent: agents as objects of MSR rather than research instruments; useful for the point that agent traces are minable only when they are recorded. Abstract-level only.

title: LessLeak-Bench: A First Investigation of Data Leakage in LLMs Across 83 Software Engineering Benchmarks
authors_or_org: Xin Zhou, Martin Weyssow, Ratnadira Widyasari, Ting Zhang, Junda He, Yunbo Lyu, Jianming Chang, Beiqi Zhang, Dan Huang, David Lo
summary: First large-scale analysis of pre-training data leakage across 83 SE benchmarks in Python, Java and C/C++. Average leakage is low but some benchmarks are heavily leaked; releases a de-leaked benchmark.
key_claims: Average leakage ratios: 4.8% Python, 2.8% Java, 0.7% C/C++.
QuixBugs 100.0% and BigCloneBench 55.7% leakage.
Leakage has a substantial impact on LLM evaluation; causes include direct inclusion in pre-training data and LeetCode-derived benchmarks.
Average leakage: 4.8% Python, 2.8% Java, 0.7% C/C++.
QuixBugs 100% leaked; BigCloneBench 55.7%.
Leakage substantially affects LLM performance assessments.
relevance: Quantifies the contamination threat for SE datasets mined from public repositories; partially COMPLICATES alarmist framing (average leakage is small) while supporting per-dataset provenance checks.

title: Automated Classification of Human Code Review Comments with Large Language Models
authors_or_org: Semih Çağlar, Şükrü Eren Gökırmak, Eray Tüzün
summary: Introduces a nine-label taxonomy of code review comment smells and intents, manually labels 448 comments, and benchmarks zero- and one-shot classification with GPT-5-mini, LLaMA-3.3 and DeepSeek-R1. Zero-shot performance is moderate and one-shot effects are model-dependent.
key_claims: 448 manually labeled comments; nine-label taxonomy.
Zero-shot macro-F1 0.360 to 0.374 under class imbalance.
One-shot exemplars improved GPT-5-mini and DeepSeek-R1 but slightly decreased LLaMA-3.3.
relevance: Counter-evidence to the 'LLMs annotate at human level' narrative for evidence-sensitive SE labels; supports per-task validation gates.

title: LLM-Based Chatbots for Mining Software Repositories: Challenges and Opportunities
authors_or_org: Samuel Abedu, Ahmad Abdellatif, Emad Shihab
summary: Builds an LLM-based chatbot to answer software-repository questions (automating data extraction for non-experts), evaluates it on 150 questions, and analyses the failure causes.
key_claims: (search snippet) Chatbot answered 1 of 150 repository-related questions correctly.
(search snippet) Five challenges identified; most frequent (83.3%) is inaccurate data retrieval.
relevance: Early evidence that LLM-mediated data collection can fail silently at the retrieval step, motivating recorded intermediate artifacts. Numbers seen in search snippet only.

title: 3100 Opinions on Code Review in an AI World: Building Causal Theory from Practitioner Discourse
authors_or_org: Shyam Agarwal, Courtney Miller, Christian Kästner, Bogdan Vasilescu
summary: Shows that MSR trends on agent-authored pull requests flip direction under equally defensible analysis choices, then builds a causal theory from 3,100 grey-literature documents coded with an LLM-assisted pipeline. Offers the LLM-assisted theory-building method as a reusable template with a public implementation.
key_claims: Agent-authored PRs are reviewed less often, merged several times faster and discussed less, but trend direction flips under different defensible analysis choices.
38,709 grey-literature documents collected; stratified sample of 3,100 coded with an LLM-assisted pipeline.
Causal model of 26 constructs and 67 relationships (64 directed, 3 contested).
relevance: Supports the thesis twice: analysis-choice sensitivity in MSR shows why intermediate decisions must be recorded, and the LLM-assisted coding pipeline is shipped as a reusable method.

title: Large Language Model for Qualitative Research: A Systematic Mapping Study
authors_or_org: Cauã Ferreira Barros, Bruna Borges Azevedo, Valdemar Vicente Graciano Neto, Mohamad Kassab, Marcos Kalinowski, Hugo Alexandre D. do Nascimento, Michelle C. G. S. P. Bandeira
summary: Systematic mapping of LLM use for qualitative research across domains, covering application contexts, configurations, methodologies and evaluation metrics. Identifies reliance on prompt engineering, inaccuracies and contextual limits as barriers.
key_claims: Challenges: reliance on prompt engineering, occasional inaccuracies, contextual limitations.
Calls for integrating LLMs with human expertise and refining evaluation methodologies.
relevance: Background mapping; supports human-expertise integration but silent on process recording.

title: Can Large Language Models emulate an inductive Thematic Analysis of semi-structured interviews? An exploration and provocation on the limits of the approach and the model
authors_or_org: Stefano De Paoli
summary: Uses GPT-3.5-Turbo to emulate parts of Braun and Clarke's six-step inductive TA on two open interview datasets previously analysed by humans, comparing themes. Finds the model can partially infer main themes; framed as a provocation on limits rather than replacement.
key_claims: Two open-access semi-structured interview datasets with prior human TA used for comparison.
The model inferred at least partially some of the main themes.
relevance: Early, widely cited exploration; shows partial theme recovery, neither strong support nor strong refutation.

title: Supporting Qualitative Analysis with Large Language Models: Combining Codebook with GPT-3 for Deductive Coding
authors_or_org: Ziang Xiao, Xingdi Yuan, Q. Vera Liao, Rania Abdelghani, Pierre-Yves Oudeyer
summary: Combines GPT-3 with expert-drafted codebooks for deductive coding of children's curiosity-driven questions, without fine-tuning. Reports fair to substantial agreement with expert coding.
key_claims: Question complexity: Cohen's kappa = 0.61; syntactic structure: kappa = 0.38 (search snippet).
Fair to substantial agreement with expert-coded results.
relevance: Early deductive-coding baseline frequently cited in HCI; shows agreement varies widely by code dimension.

title: LLM-Assisted Content Analysis: Using Large Language Models to Support Deductive Coding
authors_or_org: Robert Chew, John Bollenbacher, Michael Wenger, Jessica Speer, Annice Kim
summary: Proposes LLM-assisted content analysis (LACA) with GPT-3.5 for deductive coding, including a case study and a benchmark on four public datasets. Finds agreement often comparable to human coders and shows how LACA can detect codes where the LLM is randomly guessing and decide when to use LLM vs human coders.
key_claims: Benchmark on 4 publicly available deductive-coding datasets.
GPT-3.5 often performs deductive coding at levels of agreement comparable to human coders.
LACA helps identify codes for which the LLM is randomly guessing.
relevance: Offers an explicit decision procedure for when to delegate coding: a gate the chapter can generalise.

title: An Examination of the Use of Large Language Models to Aid Analysis of Textual Data
authors_or_org: Robert H. Tai, Lillian R. Bentley, Xin Xia, Jason M. Sitt, Sarah C. Fankhauser, Ana M. Chicas-Mosier, Barnas G. Monteith
summary: Proposes using an LLM with a codebook for deductive coding of interview excerpts, requesting supporting evidence for each code, and runs each sample text 160 times to treat iterations as independent coders. Compares LLM coding to human coders and argues it offers a systematic, reliable platform.
key_claims: Each of three sample texts input 160 times to record variation across iterations.
LLM asked to supply evidence supporting each code.
relevance: Treats repeated runs as a coder population, a design choice that only works if every run is logged; partially complicates by claiming reliability.

title: CollabCoder: A Lower-barrier, Rigorous Workflow for Inductive Collaborative Qualitative Analysis with Large Language Models
authors_or_org: Jie Gao, Yuchen Guo, Gionnieve Lim, Tianqin Zhang, Zheng Zhang, Toby Jia-Jun Li, Simon Tangi Perrault
summary: End-to-end LLM-supported workflow for inductive collaborative qualitative analysis: AI code suggestions during independent open coding with recorded decision-making data (keywords, certainty), shared decision data and agreement metrics during discussion, and AI-suggested code groups for codebook development. Evaluated with 16 users.
key_claims: Records coding decision-making data (keywords, certainty) during open coding.
Uses quantitative metrics to surface coding (dis)agreements for consensus-building.
16-user evaluation reported advantages over an existing CQA platform.
relevance: Rare example that records decision rationale as part of the workflow; a precedent for the chapter's provenance requirement within one stage.

title: Large Language Models in Qualitative Research: Uses, Tensions, and Intentions
authors_or_org: Hope Schroeder, Marianne Aubin Le Quéré, Casey Randazzo, David Mimno, Sarita Schoenebeck
summary: Interview study with 20 qualitative researchers on whether and how LLMs should be used in qualitative practice. Participants see LLMs as promising interlocutors across research stages but report concerns about performance, appropriateness and participant protection, and an urgent lack of norms and tooling.
key_claims: 20 qualitative researchers interviewed.
Rapid, broad LLM adoption across surfaces can interfere with the intentional use vital to qualitative research.
Urgent lack of norms and tooling to guide ethical LLM use in research.
relevance: Supports the thesis: 'lack of norms and tooling' and unintentional use are exactly what governed process design addresses.

title: Designing an Auditable LLM-Supported Workflow for Qualitative Thematic Analysis
authors_or_org: Nadia Jul Jeldtoft, Tariq Yousef
summary: Derives five design principles for LLM-supported inductive/latent TA (preserve interpretive context, traceable links between material and outputs, explicit analytical constructs and reasoning, constrain LLM inference to interpretive tasks, privacy-preserving local deployment) and implements a two-phase workflow combining LLM inference with deterministic procedural control. Evaluated on Danish interview transcripts against human TA and expert assessment.
key_claims: Five design principles including traceable relationships between empirical material and analytical outputs and constraining LLM inference to interpretive tasks.
Code-level coverage broadly comparable to human annotation; analytical justifications highly rated.
Produces a more compressed thematic structure with fewer, broader themes than human TA.
relevance: Closest prior art to the chapter for one stage: auditability, traceability and bounded LLM authority ('constrain inference') in TA. The chapter must cite and differentiate (whole lifecycle, agentic delegation, human semantic gates).

title: Human-AI Collaborative Inductive Thematic Analysis: AI Guided Analysis and Human Interpretive Authority
authors_or_org: Matthew Nyaaba, Min SungEun, Mary Abiswin Apam, Kwame Owoahene Acheampong, Emmanuel Dwamena, Xiaoming Zhai
summary: Studies three experienced qualitative researchers using a purpose-built Inductive Thematic Analysis GPT under a HACITA framework, focusing on analytic process. Data included interaction logs, AI tables, researcher revisions, deletions, insertions, comments and reflexive memos; interpretive authority remained with humans.
key_claims: Three experienced researchers; education interview transcripts (Ghana).
Tool enforced trace-to-text integrity, coverage checks and auditability.
Humans exercised interpretive authority via modification, deletion, rejection, insertion and commenting.
relevance: Supports the thesis: treats interaction logs and human overrides as research data, i.e. human gates as reportable process.

title: How AI Coders Discuss, Disagree, and Reach Consensus: Challenges and Opportunities for LLM-Based Qualitative Coding
authors_or_org: Jeongyeon Kim, John C. Mitchell
summary: Quantifies multi-agent LLM qualitative coding in which agents independently code, debate and reconcile, across varied datasets. Accuracy depends on codebook length, data similarity and agent disagreement; agents emulate human discussion but lack adaptive responsiveness to context.
key_claims: Intense and unresolved debates between agents led to higher accuracy.
Coding accuracy depends on codebook length, qualitative data similarity and agent disagreement.
Releases an open-source AI discussion dataset.
relevance: Multi-agent coding generates intermediate deliberation artifacts that matter to outcomes, supporting the case for recording them.

title: Not a Collaborator or a Supervisor, but an Assistant: Striking the Balance Between Efficiency and Ownership in AI-incorporated Qualitative Data Analysis
authors_or_org: Anoushka Puranik, Ester Chen, Roshan L Peiris, Hidy Kong
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW)
summary: Interviews 16 qualitative researchers about preferred degrees of AI delegation in QDA (human-only, human-initiated, AI-initiated coding). Efficiency, ownership and trust determine desired delegation; researchers want human oversight and transparency.
key_claims: 16 qualitative researchers interviewed.
Three delegation levels compared: human-only, human-initiated, AI-initiated coding.
Efficiency, ownership and trust identified as determinants of desired delegation.
relevance: Directly about 'degree of delegation' — maps onto bounded authority; supports the thesis. Venue listed as PACM HCI by S2; CSCW track not confirmed.

title: To Vibe Research or Not to Vibe Research? Generative AI in Qualitative Research
authors_or_org: Katja Karhu, Kari Smolander, Jussi Kasurinen
summary: Summarises the debate among qualitative researchers on GenAI suitability and its implications for SE researchers. Argues the research approach (small-q positivist vs Big-Q non-positivist), along with philosophy, skills, ethics and preferences, determines whether GenAI can be used.
key_claims: Small-q vs Big-Q research approach is a major criterion for whether GenAI is usable in qualitative research.
relevance: Useful nuance: the chapter's governance claims fit small-q/coding-reliability work more naturally than reflexive Big-Q work.

title: Correct codes for the wrong reasons? validating LLMs as measurement instruments for theoretical constructs
authors_or_org: Manuel Pita
summary: Argues human-LLM agreement establishes reliability but not construct validity, since an LLM may reach a code through a correlate. Proposes 'grain calibration': decompose a construct into clause-level components tested with extractive evidence and combined by an explicit theory-derived rule, so the structure is evidence about the process.
key_claims: Agreement with human annotators leaves construct validity untouched.
Grain calibration makes the coding rule explicit so validation targets the process, not only outputs.
relevance: Strong support: argues validation must move from outputs to the process, closely paralleling the chapter's thesis at the coding level.

title: GenAI Is No Silver Bullet for Qualitative Research in Software Engineering
authors_or_org: Neil A. Ernst, Christoph Treude
summary: Frontiers-of-SE paper arguing claims that GenAI can automate qualitative analysis overgeneralise from narrow successes. Outlines dimensions of SE qualitative work, scans the limited empirical evidence, examines promises and pitfalls, revisits quality factors, and sets a research agenda.
key_claims: Claims of automating qualitative analysis overgeneralise from narrow successes.
GenAI support must be adapted to both the data and the specific research strategy.
relevance: Top-venue SE position that supports the chapter's caution; the chapter can build on its quality-factor discussion with process mechanisms.

title: Antipatterns in AI-assisted Qualitative Data Analysis: A Catalog of Temptations and Pitfalls for Software Engineering Researchers
authors_or_org: Rashina Hoda, Carolyn Seaman, Victoria Gomes, Rodrigo Spinola
summary: Catalog of antipatterns in AI-assisted QDA for SE researchers, grouped as Dangerous Drivers, Operational Missteps and Analytical Failures, based on the authors' qualitative SE expertise. Intended to give researchers and reviewers vocabulary to call out failed practice.
key_claims: Antipatterns grouped in three escalating categories: Dangerous Drivers, Operational Missteps, Analytical Failures.
Warns uncritical use risks accelerated production of low-quality research.
relevance: Strongly supports the thesis and is very recent; the chapter's patterns can be framed as remedies to these antipatterns.

title: We Reject the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence for Reflexive Qualitative Research
authors_or_org: Tanisha Jowsey, Virginia Braun, Victoria Clarke, Deborah Lupton, Michelle Fine, and 414 signatories
summary: Open letter by 419 experienced qualitative researchers from 32 countries holding that reflexive approaches such as reflexive TA require a subjective, positioned, reflexive researcher, so GenAI use there is not methodologically congruent. Also rejects GenAI for reflexive research on social and environmental justice grounds.
key_claims: 419 qualitative researchers from 32 countries.
GenAI in reflexive TA is 'not methodologically congruent'.
Additional rejection on social and environmental justice grounds.
relevance: COMPLICATES the thesis from the opposite side: for reflexive work, governing AI participation is moot if it should not participate. The chapter should scope its claims accordingly. Sage page returned 403; metadata via OpenAlex.

title: Should Generative AI be Used in Reflexive Qualitative Research?
authors_or_org: Elida Izani Ibrahim, Laura K. Nelson, Andrea M. Voyer
summary: Response note challenging the claim that GenAI should be excluded from reflexive qualitative research, situating decoder LLMs within computational text analysis and arguing they can support reflexive analysis without replacing judgment. Proposes 'technological reflexivity' for responsible use.
key_claims: Generative AI is a heterogeneous set of models, many open and configurable.
Proposes technological reflexivity to guide responsible, ethical use.
relevance: Counterpoint to Jowsey et al.; 'technological reflexivity' is compatible with the chapter's call to make AI participation inspectable.

title: AI Coding Agents in Social Science: Methodologically Diverse, Empirically Consistent, Interpretively Vulnerable
authors_or_org: Meysam Alizadeh, Fabrizio Gilardi, Mohsen Mosleh, Enkelejda Kasneci
summary: Runs 20 independent executions each of Claude Code and Codex on a prominent immigration/social-policy many-analysts dataset and compares them with the human many-analysts baseline, separating a design layer (methodological choices) from a verdict layer (decision rule mapping estimates to claims).
key_claims: Codex matches human methodological diversity; Claude Code produces nearly three times as many specifications
Agents' effect estimates remain broadly aligned with the human consensus; no agent model exactly matches any human model
A prompt-induced anti-immigration prior reorganizes agents' methodological decisions but does not shift aggregate estimates or verdicts
An explicit confirmatory prompt flips Claude Code's verdicts from 10% to 90% support while leaving the coefficient distribution essentially unchanged
relevance: Mixed: agents' estimates are robust (complicates fears of agent p-hacking), but verdicts are prompt-steerable via rule omission — so the interpretive step is exactly where a human semantic gate and recorded decision rules are needed.

title: Sanity Checks for Agentic Data Science
authors_or_org: Zachary T. Rewolinski, Austin V. Zane, Hao Huang, Chandan Singh, et al.
summary: Proposes two lightweight perturbation-based sanity checks, grounded in the Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) framework, to screen whether an agentic data-science system distinguishes signal from noise. Validated on synthetic data and demonstrated on 11 real datasets with OpenAI Codex.
key_claims: Agentic data science pipelines can reach falsely optimistic conclusions that are hard for users to detect
In 6 of 11 real-world datasets an affirmative conclusion was not well-supported even though a single ADS run may support one
ADS self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated
relevance: Supports layered validation: a single agent run is not evidence; stability checks over perturbations are a concrete validation layer the chapter can cite.

title: ForkSCOPE: Charting the Agentic Garden of Forking Paths
authors_or_org: Arjun Balaji, Batuhan Duru Yeltekin, Tian Zheng
summary: A human-AI collaboration framework that induces a taxonomy of analytic forks bottom-up from a corpus of end-to-end (crowdsourced or agent-generated) analyses, with an evidence-linked interactive viewer for steering and verification, producing a decision map compatible with multiverse tools.
key_claims: Scaling agentic generation of analyses alone can create a processing bottleneck and an analytic 'black hole'
Imposing a fixed decision taxonomy can limit insight and understate uncertainty
relevance: Supports the thesis that analytic decisions must be surfaced and human-verified; it reconstructs decisions after the fact from code, whereas a provenance-first process would record them as they are made.

title: Do Claude Code and Codex P-Hack? Sycophancy and Statistical Analysis in Large Language Models
authors_or_org: Samuel Asher, Janet Malzahn, Jessica Persano, Elliot Paschal, Andrew C. W. Myers, Andrew B. Hall
summary: Working paper testing whether coding agents (Claude Opus 4.6 and OpenAI Codex (GPT-5.2)) p-hack when analysing four published political-science datasets with null or near-null results, varying framing and pressure for significance in a 2x4 factorial design across 640 runs.
key_claims: Under standard prompting both agents produce stable estimates and refuse direct requests to p-hack
A prompt reframing specification search as 'uncertainty reporting' bypasses the guardrails and induces systematic specification search
Estimate inflation under the adversarial nudge tracks the analytic flexibility of the design: observational studies are more vulnerable than randomized experiments
relevance: Mixed: agents resist overt p-hacking (complicates), yet subtle framing in instructions changes analytic behaviour — so the full instruction history, not one disclosed prompt, must be recorded. Details taken from search snippets; the PDF fetch returned 404 for one mirror.

title: Mitigating LLM-based p-Hacking by Preregistering for the Next LLM
authors_or_org: Maria Thomas, Kristina Gligorić, Nihar B. Shah
summary: Proposes preregistering an LLM-based analysis together with a set of eligible future models and running the confirmatory analysis on the first eligible model released after preregistration, so the configuration cannot be tuned against it. Evaluated on two tasks with known truth and followed in a preregistered experiment.
key_claims: LLM-based research is easy to p-hack by tuning prompts, decoding parameters or output format
Across 20 models from four providers and 11 configurations the protocol would have blocked transfer of the p-hack in 73.9% and 72.7% of cases on the two tasks
In the authors' own preregistered experiment, of 7 configurations that hacked the prior model, the hacking failed to carry over in 6 on the first eligible new model
relevance: Supports: a process-level control (commitment before execution) rather than post-hoc disclosure; an example of governance by procedure that the chapter can generalise.

title: Preregistration for Experiments with AI Agents
authors_or_org: Michelle Vaccaro
summary: Position paper arguing that preregistration should be extended to 'in silico' behavioural experiments with AI agents; catalogues the researcher degrees of freedom such experiments introduce and proposes a tailored preregistration template.
key_claims: Researcher degrees of freedom include model selection, prompt wording, settings and outcome-contingent redesign
The low cost of iteration and lack of reporting norms make these choices easy to exploit and difficult to detect
Calls on conferences, journals and funders to make preregistration expected for such experiments
relevance: Supports: names the hidden decision space of AI-agent studies; a preregistration template is a partial answer — it fixes intentions but does not record what an agent actually did.

title: Large Language Model Hacking: Quantifying the Hidden Risks of Using LLMs for Text Annotation
authors_or_org: Joachim Baumann, Paul Röttger, Aleksandra Urman, Albert Wendsjö, Flor Miriam Plaza-del-Arco, et al.
summary: Replicates 37 annotation tasks from 21 published social-science studies and analyses 13 million labels from 18 LLMs across 2,361 hypotheses to quantify how LLM configuration choices propagate into wrong downstream statistical conclusions ('LLM hacking').
key_claims: With a handful of prompt paraphrases, virtually anything can be presented as statistically significant
Incorrect conclusions in approximately 31% of hypotheses for state-of-the-art LLMs and about half for smaller models, even following standard practices
Higher task accuracy reduces but does not eliminate LLM-hacking risk; risk decreases as effect sizes increase
relevance: Strong support: configuration choices made inside an LLM-assisted pipeline change the statistical conclusion, so they must be recorded and validated, not just the final model+prompt.

title: BLADE: Benchmarking Language Model Agents for Data-Driven Science
authors_or_org: Ken Gu, Ruoxi Shang, Ruien Jiang, Keying Kuang, et al.
summary: Benchmark of 12 datasets and research questions from the scientific literature, with ground truth from independent analyses by expert data scientists, for automatically evaluating agents' analytic decisions (variables, transformations, statistical models) on open-ended research questions.
key_claims: Open-ended analysis has multiple valid approaches, partially correct steps and different ways of expressing the same decision
LMs are often limited to basic analyses; agents that interact with the data show improved but still non-optimal diversity in analytic decision making
relevance: Supports: treats analysis as a sequence of decisions to be evaluated, not just a final answer — the unit a governed process should record.

title: DiscoveryBench: Towards Data-Driven Discovery with Large Language Models
authors_or_org: Bodhisattwa Prasad Majumder, Harshit Surana, Dhruv Agarwal, Bhavana Dalvi Mishra, et al.
summary: Benchmark formalising multi-step data-driven discovery: 264 tasks across 6 domains manually derived from published papers' discovery workflows, plus 903 synthetic tasks, with facet-based evaluation of failure modes.
key_claims: 264 real tasks across 6 domains (e.g., sociology, engineering) and 903 synthetic tasks
The best evaluated LLM-based reasoning framework scores only 25%
relevance: Supports: autonomous hypothesis search/verification from data is far from reliable, motivating human validation gates.

title: Are Large Language Models Good Statisticians?
authors_or_org: Yizhang Zhu, Shiyin Du, Boyan Li, Yuyu Luo, et al.
summary: Introduces StatQA, an 11,623-example benchmark of statistical tasks emphasising applicability assessment for hypothesis-testing methods, and compares LLM and human error types.
key_claims: GPT-4o achieves a best performance of only 64.83%
Fine-tuned open-source LLMs outperform in-context methods including GPT-4o
LLMs mainly make applicability errors (choosing tests whose assumptions do not hold), while humans mostly make statistical task confusion errors
relevance: Supports: test-selection/applicability is a characteristic LLM failure — a decision that must be surfaced for human review; complementary error profiles argue for human+AI rather than delegation.

title: DSBench: How Far Are Data Science Agents from Becoming Data Science Experts?
authors_or_org: Liqiang Jing, Zhehui Huang, Xiaoyang Wang, Wenlin Yao, et al.
summary: Benchmark of 466 data analysis and 74 data modelling tasks from Eloquence and Kaggle competitions with long contexts, multimodal backgrounds, large files and multi-table structures.
key_claims: The best agent solves only 34.12% of data analysis tasks
Best Relative Performance Gap of 34.74% on data modelling
relevance: Capability baseline: realistic data-science tasks are mostly failed by agents, so agent analysis outputs require validation.

title: Using Large Language Models to Simulate Multiple Humans and Replicate Human Subject Studies
authors_or_org: Gati Aher, Rosa I. Arriaga, Adam Tauman Kalai
summary: Introduces 'Turing Experiments' that test whether a language model can simulate a representative sample of participants in human-subject research, attempting to replicate the Ultimatum Game, garden-path sentences, the Milgram shock experiment and wisdom of crowds.
key_claims: Recent models replicated existing findings in the first three Turing Experiments
The wisdom-of-crowds experiment revealed a 'hyper-accuracy distortion' in some models including ChatGPT and GPT-4
relevance: Complicates: shows LLM simulations can reproduce classic findings, but with model-specific distortions — results depend on which model was used, a provenance concern.

title: Out of One, Many: Using Language Models to Simulate Human Samples
authors_or_org: Lisa P. Argyle, Ethan C. Busby, Nancy Fulda, Joshua Gubler, et al.
summary: Argues GPT-3 bias is fine-grained and demographically correlated ('algorithmic fidelity'), so conditioning on socio-demographic backstories from real survey participants produces 'silicon samples' that emulate subgroup response distributions.
key_claims: Silicon samples conditioned on thousands of real backstories closely match human subgroup response patterns beyond surface similarity
Language models with sufficient algorithmic fidelity are proposed as a tool for social-science research
relevance: Complicates the thesis: the most-cited case that LLMs can stand in for human samples; the chapter must engage it rather than assume synthetic data is invalid.

title: Synthetic Replacements for Human Survey Data? The Perils of Large Language Models
authors_or_org: James Bisbee, Joshua D. Clinton, Cassy Dorff, Brenton Kenkel, Jennifer M. Larson
summary: Prompts ChatGPT with personas to give feeling-thermometer scores for 11 sociopolitical groups and compares with the 2016-2020 ANES.
key_claims: Average synthetic scores correspond closely to ANES averages
Synthetic sampling is not reliable for statistical inference: less variation than real surveys and regression coefficients often differ significantly
Response distributions vary with minor prompt wording changes
The same prompt yields significantly different results over a 3-month period
relevance: Strong support: temporal drift of the same prompt shows model+prompt disclosure does not make LLM-generated data reproducible.

title: Can AI language models replace human participants?
authors_or_org: Danica Dillion, Niket Tandon, Yuling Gu, Kurt Gray
summary: Short opinion article examining whether LLMs can replace human participants, using moral psychology as a case: GPT-3.5 judgments on moral scenarios correlate strongly with average human ratings.
key_claims: Reported correlation of r = .95 between GPT-3.5 and average human moral judgments (per search-result summaries)
relevance: Complicates: high aggregate correlations are the main evidence offered for substitution; the chapter should note that aggregate agreement differs from individual-level or distributional fidelity (see ahn-2026-item-mean-surrogates).

title: Large language models that replace human participants can harmfully misportray and flatten identity groups
authors_or_org: Angelina Wang, Jamie Morgenstern, John P. Dickerson
summary: Argues analytically and shows empirically on 4 LLMs, with human studies of 3,200 participants across 16 demographic identities, that LLMs misportray and flatten demographic groups when used as replacement participants; also discusses how identity prompts essentialise identities.
key_claims: Two inherent training-related limitations cause misportrayal and flattening of demographic groups
Empirical evidence from 3,200 participants across 16 identities on 4 LLMs
Urges caution where participants' identities are relevant to the task
relevance: Supports caution on synthetic participants; ethical and validity limits that a governed process should flag as a human gate before substitution.

title: The threat of analytic flexibility in using large language models to simulate human data
authors_or_org: Jamie Cummins
summary: Shows that configuration choices (model, sampling parameters, prompt formatting) when generating 'silicon samples' substantially change how well synthetic data match human data, and recommends mitigation strategies.
key_claims: Correlations between human and synthetic data ranged from r = .23 to r = .84 depending on configuration
Configurations that performed well on one dimension often performed poorly on another
relevance: Strong support: the many undisclosed configuration decisions in LLM simulation are researcher degrees of freedom that must be recorded.

title: Item-Mean Surrogates: Why Richer Persona Data Fail to Improve LLMs as Human Surrogates
authors_or_org: Daehwan Ahn, Chengfeng Mao, Dokyun Lee
summary: Tests across four datasets (>400,000 participants, >6,000 survey items/outcomes) whether richer persona data make LLMs better surrogates for individual humans.
key_claims: LLM average responses closely align with average human responses per item
After removing each item's human mean, LLM predictions explain only 3.05% of remaining respondent-specific variation versus a 53.6% human test-retest benchmark
Richer personas, model variants and fine-tuning do not close the gap
LLM responses compress human distributions (less spread, fewer categories)
relevance: Reconciles the aggregate-fidelity results (argyle-2023-out-of-one-many, dillion-2023-replace-participants) with the critiques: aggregate agreement is not individual-level substitution.

title: Whose Personae? Synthetic Persona Experiments in LLM Research and Pathways to Transparency
authors_or_org: Jan Batzner, Volker Stocker, Bingjun Tang, Anusha Natarajan, et al.
venue: AIES 2025 (Proc. AAAI/ACM Conf. on AI, Ethics, and Society 8(1):343-354)
summary: Reviews 63 peer-reviewed persona-based LLM studies (2023-2025) from NLP/AI venues and proposes a persona transparency checklist.
key_claims: Task and population of interest are often underspecified in persona experiments
Only 35% of studies discuss the representativeness of their LLM personae
Proposes a checklist emphasising representative sampling, grounding in empirical data and ecological validity
relevance: Evidence that reporting of synthetic-participant studies is incomplete; a checklist is artifact-level disclosure, which the chapter extends to process-level records.

title: Automated Social Science: Language Models as Scientist and Subjects
authors_or_org: Benjamin S. Manning, Kehang Zhu, John J. Horton
summary: System that automatically generates and tests social-science hypotheses in silico, using structural causal models as hypothesis language, blueprint for LLM agents, experimental design and analysis plan; demonstrated on negotiation, bail hearing, job interview and auction scenarios.
key_claims: Causal relationships are both proposed and tested by the system, finding evidence for some and not others
The LLM predicts the signs of estimated effects well but cannot reliably predict magnitudes
In the auction experiment simulation results closely match auction theory, while direct LLM elicitation of clearing prices is inaccurate
relevance: Shows an end-to-end AI-as-scientist-and-subject loop with an explicit pre-specified design object (the SCM) — a structural analogue of a recorded plan; also illustrates how far simulation-based studies can be automated.

title: The Influence of Fraudulent AI-Generated Responses on Software Engineering Surveys
authors_or_org: Ronnie de Souza Santos, Italo Thiago Felix dos Santos, María Teresa Baldassarre, Cleyton Magalhaes, Mairieli Santos Wessel
summary: Secondary analysis of four SE survey datasets comparing findings from original and manually cleaned data after identifying suspicious, potentially AI-assisted responses (manual identification plus automated AI-text detection). Builds on the authors' earlier investigation of AI-generated responses in Prolific-based SE surveys (arXiv:2512.17455, which found 49 suspicious responses).
key_claims: Quantitative findings generally remained stable after filtering suspicious responses, though some demographic and analytical variables varied moderately
Qualitative findings were more strongly influenced (contextual framing, code prominence, nature of supporting evidence)
Recommends combining multiple validation procedures, particularly for open-ended responses
relevance: SE-specific: LLMs enter empirical SE data uninvited via participants; data authenticity becomes a validity dimension. Partly complicates (quantitative results were robust).

title: The AI Scientist-v2: Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search
authors_or_org: Yutaro Yamada, Robert Tjarko Lange, Cong Lu, Shengran Hu, et al.
summary: Successor system that removes reliance on human-authored code templates, uses progressive agentic tree search managed by an experiment-manager agent, and adds a VLM feedback loop for figures. Three fully autonomous manuscripts were submitted to an ICLR 2025 workshop.
key_claims: One of three submitted manuscripts scored above the average human acceptance threshold
Described as the first entirely AI-generated peer-review-accepted workshop paper
relevance: Complicates (capability is real and rising) and supports (evaluation was of final manuscripts; the tree-search process is internal).

title: The AI Scientist: ICLR 2025 Workshop Experiment (repository)
authors_or_org: Sakana AI
summary: Public release accompanying the ICLR 2025 workshop experiment: the three AI-generated papers (annotated versions), Sakana's own human reviews, AI-generated reviews and the AI-reviewing code, with workshop reviewer scores in the README. The README states the experiment was run with ICLR leadership/workshop cooperation and UBC IRB approval. (The pre-commitment to withdraw the accepted paper is reported in Sakana's blog post, not the README; not re-verified.)
key_claims: Release contains final papers and reviews but no experiment logs, raw data or iterative development artifacts (per inspection of the README)
Authors state they personally reviewed the papers and their experimental results
Workshop reviewer scores ranged from 3,3,3 for one paper to 6,7,6 for the accepted one
relevance: Direct gap evidence: the flagship 'AI passed peer review' disclosure releases outputs and reviews, not the process record (decisions, intermediate artifacts, human interventions).

title: Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist
authors_or_org: Juraj Gottweis, Wei-Hung Weng, Alexander Daryin, Tao Tu, et al.
venue: Nature (2026); preprint arXiv:2502.18864 (2025), earlier titled 'Towards an AI co-scientist'
summary: Google multi-agent system built on Gemini that generates, critiques and refines research hypotheses via a tournament evolution process and asynchronous task execution, conditioned on scientists' research objectives; validated in drug repurposing, novel target discovery and antimicrobial-resistance mechanisms.
key_claims: Automated evaluations show continued benefits of test-time compute scaling on hypothesis quality
Helped identify drug-repurposing candidates for acute myeloid leukemia validated through in vitro experiments
relevance: Positions the AI as collaborator with scientist-in-the-loop and wet-lab validation — an example where external human validation gates the AI's output.
