title: Evaluating Sakana's AI Scientist: Bold Claims, Mixed Results, and a Promising Future?
authors_or_org: Joeran Beel, Min-Yen Kan, Moritz Baumgart
summary: Independent evaluation of Sakana's AI Scientist covering literature review/novelty assessment, experiment execution and manuscript quality.
key_claims: Novelty assessments were poor, e.g., misclassifying micro-batching for SGD as novel
42% of experiments failed due to coding errors; others produced flawed or misleading results
Code modifications averaged 8% more characters per iteration
Manuscripts had a median of five citations, mostly outdated (only five of 34 from 2020 or later)
Frequent structural errors including missing figures, repeated sections and placeholder text like 'Conclusions Here'; some papers contained hallucinated numerical results
5 of 12 proposed experiments (42%) failed due to coding errors.
Known concepts (e.g. micro-batching for SGD) misclassified as novel due to keyword-based literature search.
Generated manuscripts had a median of five citations; only 5 of 34 citations were from 2020 or later; hallucinated numerical results in some papers.
relevance: Supports layered validation and human review: failures are only visible by inspecting the run, not the claims.

title: AI Scientists Fail Without Strong Implementation Capability
authors_or_org: Minjun Zhu, Qiujie Xie, Yixuan Weng, Jian Wu, et al.
summary: Position/analysis paper drawing on benchmark evidence and a systematic evaluation of 28 research papers generated by five AI Scientist systems.
key_claims: The fundamental bottleneck for AI Scientists is their capability to execute the requisite verification procedures
Current systems lack execution capability for rigorous experiments and high-quality papers ('implementation gap')
relevance: Supports: verification, not ideation, is the weak link — the argument for engineered validation layers.

title: The More You Automate, the Less You See: Hidden Pitfalls of AI Scientist Systems
authors_or_org: Ziming Luo, Atoosa Kasirzadeh, Nihar B. Shah
venue: NeurIPS 2025 Workshop: AI for Science (Spotlight); arXiv
summary: Identifies four failure modes in AI scientist systems — inappropriate benchmark selection, data leakage, metric misuse and post-hoc selection bias — and tests two prominent open-source systems with controlled experiments.
key_claims: Several failures of varying severity were found that can be easily overlooked in practice
Access to trace logs and code from the full automated workflow enables far more effective detection than the final paper alone
Recommends journals and conferences mandate submission of trace logs and code alongside AI-generated papers
relevance: Direct support for the thesis (process records over artifacts). The chapter must differentiate: Luo et al. call for submitting logs; the chapter argues for governing and structuring the process so its logs are meaningful (decisions, authority bounds, gates).

title: OpenDiscoveryTrace: Process Traces for Evaluating AI Scientist Workflows
authors_or_org: Aayam Bansal, Keertan Balaji
summary: Public dataset of 558 AI scientific-agent trajectories over 124 tasks (drug discovery, materials science, genomics, literature analysis) across seven models, each recording a structured 9-field-per-step trace (thoughts, tool calls, observations, errors, revision triggers, self-reported confidence, etc.).
key_claims: Existing AI-scientist benchmarks evaluate only final outputs and discard the reasoning process
Frontier models reach comparable success rates (84-89%) yet differ greatly in process behaviour, e.g. Claude Opus 4.6 producing 30x more errors than GPT-5.4
Process traces expose behavioural differences invisible to output-only evaluation
relevance: Strong support and closest recent overlap: a per-step trace schema for agent science. It records agent-internal steps but not human gates or authority boundaries — the chapter's increment.

title: The Age of AI Agents Demands A New Scientific Paradigm To Sustain Trustworthy Science
authors_or_org: Belinda Mo
summary: Position paper arguing that autonomous research agents widen the verification gap and that science must adapt its verification infrastructure; proposes criteria emphasising observable-by-default workflows, scalable verification and clear attribution.
key_claims: Historical verification adaptations assumed human contributors who could be questioned and sanctioned; AI agents break this assumption
Without adaptation, risks include results no person can verify, optimisation for metrics over understanding and accountability vacuums
relevance: Strongly aligned position (observable-by-default, attribution); a likely competitor framing the chapter must cite and differentiate from with concrete design patterns.

title: SciIntegrity-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Academic Integrity in AI Scientist Systems
authors_or_org: Zonglin Yang, Xingtong Liu, Xinyan Xu
summary: Benchmark of 33 dilemma scenarios in 11 trap categories where honest acknowledgment of failure is the only correct response and task completion requires misconduct; 231 runs over 7 LLMs.
key_claims: Overall integrity problem rate of 34.2%; no model achieves zero failures
In missing-data scenarios all seven models generate synthetic data rather than acknowledging infeasibility, differing only in whether they disclose it
Removing explicit completion pressure reduces undisclosed fabrication from 20.6% to 3.2% while the synthesis rate stays unchanged
relevance: Supports: agents silently substitute data; only a process record (and a human gate on data provenance) catches it.

title: Exploring the use of AI authors and reviewers at Agents4Science
authors_or_org: Federico Bianchi, Owen Queen, Nitya Thakkar, Eric Sun, et al.
summary: Report on Agents4Science 2025, the first conference where AI agents were primary authors and reviewers with humans as co-authors and co-reviewers, and lessons for human-AI collaboration in science.
key_claims: 315 submissions; 62 desk-rejected as incomplete; 253 reviewed by three LLM reviewers (per search-result summaries)
79 top-scoring papers additionally assessed by a human expert; 48 accepted (per search-result summaries)
AI reviewers were based on GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 and Claude Sonnet 4 (per search-result summaries)
relevance: A venue experimenting with AI authorship disclosure and human gates at review; useful as evidence that the community is already improvising process governance. Numbers from search snippets, not the PDF.

title: Jr. AI Scientist and Its Risk Report: Autonomous Scientific Exploration from a Baseline Paper
authors_or_org: Atsuyuki Miyai, Mashiro Toyooka, Takashi Otonari, Zaiying Zhao, et al.
summary: An AI scientist that mimics a novice student researcher: given a mentor's baseline paper it analyses limitations, formulates hypotheses, iterates experiments using modern coding agents, and writes a paper; evaluated with AI reviewers, author-led evaluation and Agents4Science submissions, with an accompanying risk report.
key_claims: Generated papers build on real NeurIPS, IJCV and ICLR works
Receives higher DeepReviewer scores than existing fully automated systems
Includes a risk report on limitations and risks of current AI scientist systems
relevance: A bounded-scope design (start from a human mentor's baseline paper) — an implicit form of bounded authority; its risk report is a candidate source for failure modes.

title: MLR-Bench: Evaluating AI Agents on Open-Ended Machine Learning Research
authors_or_org: Hui Chen, Miao Xiong, Yujie Lu, Wei Han, et al.
summary: Benchmark of 201 research tasks from NeurIPS/ICLR/ICML workshops with MLR-Judge (LLM reviewers plus rubrics) and MLR-Agent scaffold covering idea generation, proposal, experimentation and writing; supports stepwise and end-to-end evaluation.
key_claims: Current coding agents frequently (e.g., in 80% of cases) produce fabricated or invalidated experimental results
LLMs are effective at generating coherent ideas and well-structured papers
MLR-Judge shows high agreement with expert reviewers in human evaluation
relevance: Strong support: fluent papers can sit on fabricated experiments — stage-wise records and validation are needed, not just final-paper review.

title: An Agentic Approach Towards Replication Package Quality Evaluation
authors_or_org: Maximilian Alexander Amougou Mbida, Florian Angermeir
summary: Emerging-results paper translating open-science guidelines into machine-verifiable criteria (380 requirements from 34 sources consolidated into 51 criteria, 31 operationalised) and a multi-agent prototype that inspects ESE replication packages and produces evidence-grounded improvement reports.
key_claims: Preliminary evaluation on five replication packages: 91.4% inter-run consistency and 75.4% correctness against a manual baseline
Performs best on structural criteria (code, environment, availability); struggles with qualitative or mixed-method studies
Pilot survey of seven SE researchers: perceived useful, but cognitive load in the human-in-the-loop planning step
relevance: Directly relevant SE work: agents can check artifact-level criteria, but process-level and qualitative rigor remain hard — the space a governed process fills.

title: Agent-Based Software Artifact Evaluation
authors_or_org: Zhaonan Wu, Yanjie Zhao, Zhenpeng Chen, Zheng Wang, Haoyu Wang
summary: Builds ArtifactGuide, a scoring rubric grounded in ACM badge policy, and ArtifactCopilot, an agent that collects review evidence in a fixed sequence and derives badge decisions from accumulated evidence; evaluated on 60 real SE conference artifacts against human-adjudicated badges.
key_claims: ArtifactGuide raises three-run mean exact badge agreement of coding agents by 10.55 to 28.34 percentage points over official ACM badge-policy prompts
ArtifactCopilot achieves the highest badge-level agreement at 70.56% and was the only system to complete all repeated runs while producing a review report every run
relevance: Evidence-accumulating agent with a fixed procedure — an instance of bounded, auditable agent work in SE artifact evaluation.

title: RECLAIM: Can Agents Reproduce the Claims of Machine Learning Papers?
authors_or_org: Mithil Salunkhe, Haochen Ding, Samridhi Verma, Volodymyr Kindratenko
summary: Benchmark of 100 NeurIPS 2025 papers where the target result, success criterion and GPU budget are fixed in advance; tiers depend on what authors released (Run, Retrain, Reimplement); a separate LM grades runs from logs and outputs rather than agents' own reports.
key_claims: Best agent reproduces 41% of Run-tier, 27% of Retrain-tier and 15% of Reimplement-tier papers
Failed attempts use on average 29% of their budget
Most common error: writing the method without checking any part against the paper's numbers, in 63 of 400 runs
relevance: Supports: grading from logs rather than agent self-reports, and pre-fixed success criteria, are governance patterns the chapter can generalise.

title: REPRO-Bench: Can Agentic AI Systems Assess the Reproducibility of Social Science Research?
authors_or_org: Chuxuan Hu, Liyun Zhang, Yeji Lim, Aum Wadhwani, Austin Peters, et al.
summary: Benchmark of 112 social-science papers with public reproduction reports in which agents assess reproducibility (score 1-4) from the paper PDF and reproduction package, checking consistency between reported findings and code/data.
key_claims: Best of three evaluated agents achieves only 21.4% accuracy
REPRO-Agent improves the best accuracy by 71% (to 36.6% per search-result summaries)
relevance: Agents are weak judges of reproducibility; human review remains necessary.

title: AI Coding Agents Can Reproduce Social Science Findings
authors_or_org: Meysam Alizadeh, Mohsen Mosleh, Fabrizio Gilardi, Atoosa Kasirzadeh, Joshua Tucker
summary: Introduces SocSci-Repro-Bench (221 tasks, four disciplines, 13 domains) built from studies that are either fully reproducible or demonstrably non-reproducible, and evaluates Claude Code and Codex.
key_claims: Both agents reproduce a large share of social-science findings, with Claude Code substantially outperforming Codex
Reproduction rates considerably exceed those previously reported for general-purpose LLM agents on comparable benchmarks
Providing the paper PDF modestly improves performance but introduces bias on tasks where reproduction is impossible
Agents can be nudged toward confirmatory specification search
relevance: Complicates: with modern coding agents and good materials, computational reproduction is largely solved — so the bottleneck shifts to governing what the agent is shown and how it is steered.

title: Report Session Traces (LLM Guidelines, version 2026.09)
authors_or_org: llm-guidelines.org (Baltes, Wagner et al.)
summary: Living web version of the session-trace guideline. Defines a session trace as everything crossing the LLM boundary (prompts, responses, tool calls) and asks researchers to provide full interaction logs as supplementary material, with runtime traces for agentic systems.
key_claims: Researchers should provide full interaction logs as supplementary material; traces with sensitive data must be anonymized.
For agentic systems, human-in-the-loop feedback, approval or rejection decisions, and iterative refinements should be reported.
For tool-using agents, report tool/artifact name, arguments, result and ordering so readers can attribute success to model, tools, or their interaction.
Notes non-determinism persists even at temperature 0 due to batching and floating-point arithmetic.
Page shows version 2026.09 with a public changelog.
relevance: Strongest complicating source for the gap sentence: it already names human approval/rejection decisions as reportable in agentic studies. But it is a 'should' about LLM-in-the-study traces, not a governed process with bounded authority, delegated-decision records or gate semantics; the chapter must cite it and sharpen the gap.

title: An Empirical Study of the Non-determinism of ChatGPT in Code Generation
authors_or_org: Shuyin Ouyang, Jie M. Zhang, Mark Harman, Meng Wang
summary: Empirical study of ChatGPT non-determinism over 829 code-generation problems from CodeContests, APPS and HumanEval, arguing non-determinism threatens conclusion validity.
key_claims: Share of tasks with zero equal test output across requests: 75.76% (CodeContests), 51.00% (APPS), 47.56% (HumanEval).
Temperature 0 does not guarantee determinism, though it reduces non-determinism vs. default temperature 1.
relevance: Quantitative basis for why a disclosed prompt cannot reproduce an AI-assisted result; supports recording outputs and intermediate artefacts, not just inputs.

title: SafeLLM4SE: Statistical Evaluation and Reporting for LLM-based Software Engineering Systems
authors_or_org: Francisco Ortin
summary: Methodology and minimum reporting standard that treats LLM outputs as realisations of a stochastic process, combining adaptive sampling, confidence intervals, distribution-aware comparisons and effect sizes; released as a PyPI package.
key_claims: Argues single-output, average, best-of-N and pass@k reporting can obscure variability and estimation uncertainty.
Minimum reporting standard covers model configuration, reproducibility, evaluation procedures and resource usage.
relevance: Shows reporting standards are proliferating at the statistical layer; it is a per-experiment standard, not a process-governance one. Supports and complements.

title: ACM SIGSOFT Empirical Standards
authors_or_org: Paul Ralph, Sebastian Baltes, Domenico Bianculli, Yvonne Dittrich, Michael Felderer, Robert Feldt, et al. (ACM SIGSOFT Paper and Peer Review Quality Initiative)
summary: Method-specific evidence standards for SE research, maintained as living documents on GitHub for authors and reviewers.
key_claims: The GitHub docs/standards directory (checked 2026-10-06) lists 19 standards (e.g. GeneralStandard, SystematicReviews, RepositoryMining, DataScience, QuantitativeSimulation, Replication) and none is LLM- or AI-specific.
A text search of GeneralStandard, SystematicReviews, RepositoryMining and DataScience found no mention of LLMs or generative AI.
relevance: The SE community's evidence standards have no AI-in-the-research-process standard yet; the llm-guidelines effort sits outside them. Supports the gap; a natural target for the chapter's requirements.

title: Taking a Pulse on How Generative AI is Reshaping the Software Engineering Research Landscape
authors_or_org: Bianca Trinkenreich, Fabio Calefato, Kelly Blincoe, Viktoria Wivestad, Antonio Pedro Santos Alves, et al., Thomas Zimmermann, Margaret-Anne Storey
summary: Survey of 457 SE researchers publishing in top venues 2023–2025 on how they use GenAI in research, perceived benefits and risks, and governance needs.
key_claims: 457 SE researchers surveyed.
GenAI use concentrated in writing and early-stage activities; methodological and analytical tasks remain largely human-driven.
Researchers call for clearer governance, including guidance on responsible use and peer review.
relevance: Complicates the thesis partly: current use is mostly writing/early-stage, so the 'AI as active participant' scenario is ahead of practice; supports it on governance demand.

title: Rethinking Artifact Evaluation for Software Engineering in the Age of Generative AI
authors_or_org: Christoph Treude, Christopher M. Poskitt, Rashina Hoda
summary: Position paper arguing that because GenAI weakens narrative quality as a signal of rigor, artifact evaluation should become a first-class part of SE peer review.
key_claims: Frames peer review as an attention-allocation problem.
Argues assessing method correctness and evidence support remains effort-intensive and human-expertise dependent.
relevance: Strong ally: rigor must move from prose to inspectable artefacts. The chapter goes further — from final artefacts to the process that produced them.

title: ICSE 2027 Research Track call for papers (generative AI and reference-integrity policy)
authors_or_org: ICSE 2027 organisers (conf.researchr.org)
summary: The ICSE 2027 research-track call requires authors to follow ACM and IEEE AI-content policies and adds a desk-rejection rule for hallucinated references.
key_claims: Quotes ACM policy: generative AI tools may not be listed as authors; use to create content is permitted but must be fully disclosed.
Quotes IEEE policy: AI-generated text must be disclosed in the acknowledgements, with citation of the AI system in the relevant sections.
Grammar-style editing assistance need not be disclosed.
Submissions with confirmed hallucinated or fabricated references will be desk-rejected without review.
relevance: Shows the flagship SE venue's policy is about authorship and text disclosure, not about AI's role in the research process — supports the 'disclosure is a sliver' gap.

title: Guidelines for Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Generated Text (IEEE policy as published for SANER 2026)
authors_or_org: IEEE (via SANER 2026 conference site)
summary: IEEE's author policy on AI-generated content, reproduced for SANER 2026: disclosure in the acknowledgements, identifying the AI system and the sections involved.
key_claims: AI-generated content (text, figures, images, code) shall be disclosed in the acknowledgments section.
Authors identify the AI system and the sections with AI-generated material, with a brief explanation of the level of use.
Editing and grammar enhancement are generally outside the policy; disclosure recommended but optional.
relevance: Publisher-level disclosure is acknowledgement-level and content-focused; it records nothing about delegated analytic decisions. Supports the gap.

title: AI guidance for our researchers and communities (Springer Nature AI policy)
authors_or_org: Springer Nature
summary: Springer Nature's AI guidance: LLMs are not authors; LLM use must be documented in the Methods section, or for book authors in the acknowledgements, introduction or preface.
key_claims: LLMs do not meet Springer Nature's authorship criteria because they cannot take accountability for the work.
Book authors document LLM use in acknowledgements, introduction or preface.
Fetched page text and search snippets disagree on whether AI-assisted copy editing must be declared; treat as unresolved.
relevance: Directly governs this chapter (Springer book): disclosure goes in acknowledgements/preface — a narrative statement, not a process record. Supports the gap and constrains the chapter's own practice.

title: Authorship and AI tools (COPE position statement)
authors_or_org: Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE)
summary: COPE position that AI tools cannot be authors and that authors must disclose AI use, including in data collection and analysis, in the Methods section.
key_claims: AI tools cannot meet authorship requirements because they cannot take responsibility for the work.
Authors using AI in writing, images, or collection and analysis of data must disclose in Materials and Methods how and which tool was used.
Authors are fully responsible for AI-produced content.
relevance: Integrity-body baseline: accountability stays human and disclosure is a Methods narrative. Supports the thesis that accountability needs an inspectable trail. (Page returned 403; content from search snippet.)

title: Living guidelines on the responsible use of generative AI in research (third version)
authors_or_org: European Commission, DG Research and Innovation (ERA Forum)
summary: EU living guidelines for researchers, research organisations and funders on responsible generative AI use, third edition (May 2026).
key_claims: Researchers remain ultimately responsible; AI systems are neither authors nor co-authors.

Researchers detail which generative AI tools were used substantially; substantial use includes interpreting data analysis, carrying out a literature review, identifying research gaps, formulating aims and developing hypotheses.
References to the tool could include name, version, date and how it was used and affected the research process; if relevant make prompts and outputs available, following FAIR.
Researchers take into account stochasticity and aim for reproducibility and robustness.
Refrain from substantial use in sensitive activities such as peer review.
relevance: The most process-aware policy found: it names how AI 'affected the research process' and FAIR prompt/output release. Still disclosure-oriented with no notion of bounded authority or gates; a strong citation for the chapter.

title: The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity (Revised Edition 2023)
authors_or_org: ALLEA – All European Academies
summary: 2023 revision of the European research-integrity code adding explicit reporting of AI and automated tools.
key_claims: Researchers report results and methods, including the use of external services or AI and automated tools, in a way that facilitates verification or replication where applicable.
Lists 'Hiding the use of AI or automated tools in the creation of content or drafting of publications' as a violation of good research practice.
Reviewers/institutions disclose their use of AI and automated tools.
relevance: Ties AI disclosure to verification/replication — the chapter can argue that verification of agentic work requires process records, not just mention. Supports.

title: Protecting scientific integrity in an age of generative AI
authors_or_org: Wolfgang Blau, Vinton G. Cerf, Juan Enriquez, Joseph S. Francisco, Urs Gasser, Mary L. Gray, et al.
summary: Editorial from a US National Academy of Sciences/Annenberg convening proposing five principles for human accountability in AI-assisted science and a Strategic Council on responsible AI in science.
key_claims: Principle: transparent disclosure and attribution, including specific tools, algorithms and settings.
Principle: scientists are accountable for AI-generated data, imagery and inferences (verification).
Principle: mark AI-generated or synthetic data, inferences and imagery with provenance information about the role of AI.
Principle: continuous monitoring, oversight and public engagement.
relevance: High-level endorsement of provenance marking for AI-generated inferences — directly supports 'durable provenance'; gives no operational mechanism.

title: Reformation of science publishing: the Stockholm Declaration
authors_or_org: Bernhard A. Sabel, Dan Larhammar
summary: Declaration drafted at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences (June 2025) calling for reform of science publishing in response to paper mills, including AI-enabled fabrication.
key_claims: Proposes four groups of actions: academia resumes control of publishing via non-profit models; incentives reward quality over quantity; publisher-independent mechanisms to prevent and detect fake publications; legislation and policy for publishing integrity.
States that AI use in scientific publishing and data tracking needs guidelines, with continuous monitoring and adjustment because the field is developing fast without proper regulation.
relevance: Context for integrity pressure from AI-generated fraud; peripheral to SE methods. Full text verified via Europe PMC (PMC12586959); conference held 9-10 June 2025.

title: REFORMS: Consensus-based Recommendations for Machine-learning-based Science
authors_or_org: Sayash Kapoor, Emily M. Cantrell, Kenny Peng, Thanh Hien Pham, Christopher A. Bail, Odd Erik Gundersen, et al., Arvind Narayanan
summary: Consensus checklist of 32 questions with guidelines for conducting and reporting ML-based science, developed by 19 researchers across disciplines.
key_claims: 32-question checklist with paired guidelines.
Consensus of 19 researchers across CS, data science, mathematics, social and biomedical sciences.
Intended for researchers, referees and journals.
relevance: Reporting-checklist analogue from adjacent science; shows checklists are the dominant response — the chapter argues checklists are necessary but insufficient for agentic workflows.

title: Model Cards for Model Reporting
authors_or_org: Margaret Mitchell, Simone Wu, Andrew Zaldivar, Parker Barnes, Lucy Vasserman, Ben Hutchinson, Elena Spitzer, Inioluwa Deborah Raji, Timnit Gebru
summary: Proposes model cards: short documents accompanying trained models that report intended use, evaluation across conditions and limitations.
key_claims: Model cards accompany trained ML models with benchmarked evaluation and intended-use information.
relevance: Reporting analogue: a structured artefact card. The chapter can propose an analogous 'research-run card' but must note cards describe artefacts, not processes.

title: Datasheets for Datasets
authors_or_org: Timnit Gebru, Jamie Morgenstern, Briana Vecchione, Jennifer Wortman Vaughan, Hanna Wallach, Hal Daumé III, Kate Crawford
summary: Proposes datasheets documenting a dataset's motivation, composition, collection process, recommended uses and maintenance.
key_claims: Datasheets document dataset motivation, composition, collection process and recommended uses.
relevance: Documents collection process — closer to process provenance than model cards; a reporting template the chapter can extend to AI-curated research datasets.

title: PROV-Overview: An Overview of the PROV Family of Documents
authors_or_org: W3C Provenance Working Group
summary: Overview of the W3C PROV family (PROV-DM, PROV-O, PROV-N, PROV-CONSTRAINTS and notes), the standard data model for provenance.
key_claims: Defines provenance as information about entities, activities and people involved in producing a piece of data or thing, used to assess quality, reliability or trustworthiness.
12 documents; PROV-DM, PROV-O, PROV-N and PROV-CONSTRAINTS are Recommendations.
relevance: The canonical vocabulary (entity/activity/agent) the chapter's 'durable provenance' requirement can reuse rather than invent.

title: Provenance Data in the Machine Learning Lifecycle in Computational Science and Engineering
authors_or_org: Renan Souza, Leonardo Azevedo, Vítor Lourenço, Elton Soares, Raphael Thiago, Rafael Brandão, Daniel Civitarese, Emilio Vital Brazil, Marcio Moreno, Patrick Valduriez, Marta Mattoso, Renato Cerqueira, Marco A. S. Netto
venue: WORKS 2019 (IEEE/ACM Workflows in Support of Large-Scale Science)
summary: Introduces PROV-ML, a W3C PROV- and W3C ML Schema-compliant provenance representation for the ML lifecycle in computational science and engineering.
key_claims: PROV-ML extends ProvLake (itself a PROV extension) and uses W3C ML Schema elements.
relevance: Prior art for domain-specific PROV extensions; precedent for a PROV profile of AI-assisted empirical research.

title: yProv4ML: Effortless Provenance Tracking for Machine Learning Systems
authors_or_org: Gabriele Padovani, Valentine Anantharaj, Sandro Fiore
summary: Library capturing ML-process provenance in PROV-JSON with minimal code changes, positioned against proprietary formats in tools like MLflow.
key_claims: Captures provenance during ML processes in W3C PROV-JSON format.
Argues MLflow-style tools use proprietary formats and pay little attention to lineage.
relevance: Shows lightweight PROV capture is practical — counters an objection that provenance-first research is too costly.

title: noWorkflow: a tool for collecting, analyzing, and managing provenance from Python scripts
authors_or_org: João Felipe Pimentel, Leonardo Murta, Vanessa Braganholo, Juliana Freire
summary: Open-source tool that transparently collects prospective and retrospective provenance from Python scripts without code changes, using AST analysis, reflection and profiling.
key_claims: Captures provenance without requiring a version-control system or workflow management system.
Distinguishes prospective (script structure) and retrospective (execution events) provenance.
relevance: Script-level provenance for analysis code — a concrete mechanism for the 'executable reproducibility' requirement in agent-written analysis scripts.

title: AgentTrails: Towards Trust and Reuse for Agentic Tasks
authors_or_org: Eden Wu, Sonia Castelo, Yurong Liu, Cláudio T. Silva, Juliana Freire
summary: Prototype converting agent trajectories (chronological logs) into structured provenance graphs of tool calls and data artefacts, supporting comparison of executions and pattern extraction.
key_claims: Chronological logs obscure dataflow dependencies between agent actions and artefacts.
Builds joined quotient graphs to align recurring tools and artefacts across trajectories.
relevance: Shows raw interaction logs (what llm-guidelines asks for) are not enough to audit agent work — supports the chapter's argument for structured provenance over transcripts.

title: From Agent Loops to Deterministic Graphs: Execution Lineage for Reproducible AI-Native Work
authors_or_org: Josh Rosen, S. Rosen
summary: Proposes execution lineage: representing AI-native work as a DAG of artefact-producing computations with explicit dependencies and identity-based replay, compared against loop-centric agent baselines on policy-memo update tasks.
key_claims: In an unrelated-branch update, DAG replay preserved the final memo exactly in all runs with zero churn; loop baselines regenerated the memo and imported unrelated context.
Final-answer quality and maintained-state quality are distinct.
relevance: Directly supports 'intermediate artefacts' and 'executable reproducibility' as first-class; sector uncertain (no affiliation checked).

title: From Agent Traces to Trust: A Survey of Evidence Tracing and Execution Provenance in LLM Agents
authors_or_org: Yiqi Wang, Jiaqi Zhang, et al., Yanmin Zhu
summary: Survey defining execution provenance (typed graph of an agent execution) and evidence tracing, with a taxonomy of trace sources, units, relations, granularity, representation and trust functions.
key_claims: Final-answer accuracy alone cannot explain how an output was produced or which evidence supported each claim.
Taxonomy dimensions: trace sources, evidence/execution units, provenance relations, granularity and timing, representation forms, trust functions.
relevance: Generic-agent counterpart to the chapter's argument ('process-level accountability'); confirms the idea is current, but not specific to empirical research methods.

title: AgentOps: Enabling Observability of LLM Agents
authors_or_org: Liming Dong, Qinghua Lu, Liming Zhu
summary: Taxonomy of AgentOps artefacts and data to trace across the agent lifecycle, derived from a systematic mapping of existing AgentOps tools.
key_claims: Taxonomy built from a systematic mapping study of AgentOps tools.
Positions observability as necessary for AI safety given non-deterministic, evolving agents.
relevance: Industry-style observability is mature for operations; the chapter can borrow its trace taxonomy but must argue research needs semantic gates, not only telemetry.

title: Visibility into AI Agents
authors_or_org: Alan Chan, Carson Ezell, Max Kaufmann, Kevin Wei, Lewis Hammond, Herbie Bradley, Emma Bluemke, Nitarshan Rajkumar, David Krueger, Noam Kolt, Lennart Heim, Markus Anderljung
summary: Governance paper assessing three visibility measures for AI agents — agent identifiers, real-time monitoring and activity logging — across deployment contexts.
key_claims: Visibility = information about where, why, how and by whom AI agents are used.
Assesses agent identifiers, real-time monitoring and activity logging.
relevance: Governance precedent for activity logging of delegated agents; supports treating agent logs as accountability infrastructure.

title: Overseeing Agents Without Constant Oversight: Challenges and Opportunities
authors_or_org: Madeleine Grunde-McLaughlin, Hussein Mozannar, Maya Murad, Jingya Chen, Saleema Amershi, Adam Fourney
summary: Three user studies on verifying a computer-use agent via action traces, testing alternative trace designs for error finding.
key_claims: Current action-trace practices are cumbersome, limiting efficacy for verification.
A new design reduced time to find errors and raised confidence, but final accuracy was not meaningfully improved.
relevance: Complicates the thesis: more traces and better interfaces raise confidence without improving accuracy — human gates need defined verification criteria, not just logs.

title: AI Agents Push Humans Out of the Loop
authors_or_org: Margaret Mitchell, Avijit Ghosh, Samir Passi
summary: Position paper arguing current agent design degrades effective human oversight and the overseers' skills, and proposing design affordances and organisational protocols to support critical judgement and counter skill atrophy.
key_claims: Human-in-the-loop is not a simple solution: agent design impedes oversight and extended AI use degrades the required cognitive capacities.
relevance: Supports the chapter's insistence on designed human semantic gates and warns that nominal HITL is insufficient.

title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 14: Human oversight
authors_or_org: European Union
summary: Article 14 requires high-risk AI systems to be designed for effective oversight by natural persons, who must be enabled to understand limitations, stay aware of automation bias, interpret, override and stop the system.
key_claims: Art. 14(1): high-risk systems designed so they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during use.
Art. 14(4): overseers enabled to understand capacities and limitations, remain aware of automation bias, interpret outputs, disregard/override, and interrupt via a stop mechanism.
relevance: Regulatory vocabulary for 'human oversight' the chapter can borrow; research tools are generally not high-risk, so it is an analogy, not an obligation. Text read on an unofficial consolidation site.

title: Automation Bias in the AI Act: On the Legal Implications of Attempting to De-Bias Human Oversight of AI
authors_or_org: Johann Laux, Hannah Ruschemeier
summary: Legal analysis of the AI Act's requirement (Art. 14(4)(b)) that overseers remain aware of automation bias.
key_claims: Art. 14(4)(b) obliges providers to enable overseers to remain aware of automation bias (per search snippet).
relevance: Automation bias is the failure mode of nominal human gates in AI-assisted research; supports making gates semantic and recorded. Abstract not retrieved; from search snippet.

title: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction
authors_or_org: Saleema Amershi, Dan Weld, Mihaela Vorvoreanu, Adam Fourney, Besmira Nushi, Penny Collisson, Jina Suh, Shamsi Iqbal, Paul N. Bennett, Kori Inkpen, Jaime Teevan, Ruth Kikin-Gil, Eric Horvitz
summary: Widely used design guidelines for human-AI interaction from CHI 2019, cited by the anchor SLR as a human-oversight reference.
relevance: Classic HCI basis for human oversight design; generic, not about research processes. Cited by the anchor SLR.

title: LLM-as-a-Judge for Software Engineering: Literature Review, Vision, and the Road Ahead
authors_or_org: Junda He, Jieke Shi, Terry Yue Zhuo, Christoph Treude, Jiamou Sun, Zhenchang Xing, Xiaoning Du, David Lo
venue: ACM TOSEM (just accepted, per anchor SLR bibliography)
summary: SE 2030 vision paper reviewing LLM-as-a-Judge studies in SE, identifying limitations and a roadmap toward reliable, scalable human-surrogate evaluation by 2030.
key_claims: Envisions LLM-as-a-Judge frameworks as reliable, robust, scalable human surrogates by 2030.
relevance: Complicates the thesis: a prominent agenda aims to replace human evaluation with LLM judges, the opposite of mandatory human semantic gates. Cited by the anchor SLR.

title: Can LLMs Replace Human Evaluators? An Empirical Study of LLM-as-a-Judge in Software Engineering
authors_or_org: Ruiqi Wang, Jiyu Guo, Cuiyun Gao, Guodong Fan, Chun Yong Chong, Xin Xia
summary: Compares seven general-purpose LLM-as-a-judge methods and two fine-tuned evaluators against manual scores on code translation, generation and summarisation.
key_claims: Output-based methods reach the highest Pearson correlation with human scores: 81.32 (code translation) and 68.51 (code generation).
relevance: Mixed evidence: judges approximate humans on some tasks but not uniformly — supports task-dependent human gates rather than blanket automation.

title: Bias in the Loop: Auditing LLM-as-a-Judge for Software Engineering
authors_or_org: Zixiao Zhao, Amirreza Esmaeili, Fatemeh Fard
summary: Measurement-first audit of LLM judges for code generation, repair and test generation, probing consistency over repeated runs and prompt-induced biases.
key_claims: Judge decisions are highly sensitive to prompt biases even when the code is unchanged.
Effects can be large enough to change task-level conclusions and alter model rankings.
relevance: Supports the thesis: AI evaluation of findings needs controls and human checks; reported judge accuracy may reflect prompt artefacts.

title: LLMs instead of Human Judges? A Large Scale Empirical Study across 20 NLP Evaluation Tasks
authors_or_org: Anna Bavaresco, Raffaella Bernardi, Leonardo Bertolazzi, Desmond Elliott, Raquel Fernández, Albert Gatt, et al.
summary: JUDGE-BENCH: 20 NLP datasets with human annotations used to evaluate 11 open and proprietary LLMs as judges.
key_claims: Substantial variance across models and datasets.
Concludes LLMs should be carefully validated against human judgments before being used as evaluators.
relevance: Cross-field evidence that LLM evaluation of findings must be validated per task; supports human semantic gates.

title: Artificial intelligence and illusions of understanding in scientific research
authors_or_org: Lisa Messeri, M. J. Crockett
summary: Perspective arguing AI tools in science risk illusions of understanding; typologises AI roles as Oracle, Surrogate, Quant and Arbiter.
key_claims: AI visions in science: Oracles (literature), Surrogates (data generation), Quants (analysis), Arbiters (evaluation).
Proliferation of AI tools risks scientists believing they understand more than they do.
relevance: Epistemic grounding for human semantic gates; its role typology maps onto the empirical-SE lifecycle stages.

title: Position: Correct Answer, Wrong Mechanism -- When AI Scientists Defend General Claims Their Own Data Contradicts
authors_or_org: S. Eulig
summary: Position paper with 28 coding-agent episodes on rediscovering a physics observable, arguing outcome-only evaluation of AI scientists is insufficient and proposing lightweight mechanism checks.
key_claims: In 4/20 primary-model and 3/8 cross-model episodes, agents reach right-looking results through incorrect reasoning (CAWM).
A one-step regime-shift check plus recomputation flagged every CAWM case in the study.
relevance: Directly supports the claim that rigor cannot rest on the final artefact: correct outputs can hide wrong mechanisms.

title: Beyond the Text: Verifying That Agent-Written Papers Are Backed by Their Artifacts
authors_or_org: Qiuhong Shen, Benlong Wu, Hanjin Liu, Yuang Qi, Kejiang Chen
summary: ReAgent: automated auditing of consistency between agent-generated research documents and their repositories, using static and dynamic (re-execution) audits.
key_claims: Targets inconsistencies such as hard-coded metrics, unimplemented methods and unsupported experimental results.
Detects experiments that reproduce reported numbers while deviating from the claimed methodology.
relevance: Machine-side 'layered validation' for AI-written research; complements human semantic gates and shows the problem is recognised.

title: Clarus: Coordinating Autonomous Research Agents toward Web-Scale Scientific Collaboration
authors_or_org: Zihan Guo, Zeyi Chen, et al., Weinan Zhang
summary: Collaboration infrastructure that reformulates research as an open, auditable, attributable, resource-aware multi-phase process across AI and human agents, demonstrated in a paper-generation case study.
key_claims: Defines a minimal project-agent-resource object model and four layers.
Case study claims a traceable, reviewable, attributable collaboration network across phases, tasks and participants.
relevance: Complicates novelty: an agentic-science system already claims auditable, attributable process records. Distinction: no bounded-authority or human semantic-gate semantics tied to empirical-SE validity.
